The 'anawim in the Psalms and Prophets are not simply the materially destitute — they are those who, being without resources or power, depend entirely on God. "In spirit" specifies the orientation: these are people whose inner posture is that of the 'anawim, whether or not they are materially poor. They know they have nothing to bring. The kingdom of heaven belongs to them — present tense (estin), not future. The arriving kingdom is theirs now.

"Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" (v. 4). Again Isaiah 61 stands behind this. Isaiah 61:2-3 speaks of comforting "all who mourn" and giving them "a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning." The mourning in Isaiah's context is Israel's mourning over exile, destruction, and national suffering. Jesus declares that those who are presently in this state of grief — over the condition of God's people, over sin, over the brokenness of the world — will be comforted. The passive "shall be comforted" (paraklethesontai) is a divine passive: God will comfort them.

"Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth" (v. 5). This is a direct quotation of Psalm 37:11 (LXX 36:11): "the meek shall inherit the earth/land" (hoi praeis kleronomesousin ten gen). In Psalm 37, the meek (praeis/'anawim) are contrasted with the wicked who prosper temporarily. The psalm's argument is that the wicked will be cut off, but those who wait on the LORD will possess the land. The word gen can mean either "land" (specifically the promised land of Israel) or "earth" (the whole world). In the context of the arriving kingdom, Jesus extends the promise: the meek — those who do not seize power by force — will inherit, not just a strip of territory, but the earth itself.

"Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied" (v. 6). "Righteousness" (dikaiosyne) appeared in Jesus's first words in this document (3:15, "to fulfill all righteousness"). The author has already established this word as conformity to God's will and purposes. Those who hunger and thirst for this — who ache for things to be set right according to God's design — will be "satisfied" (chortasthesontai), a word used for being filled to satiation, often used of feeding animals until they can eat no more. The promise is emphatic: not a partial satisfaction, but a complete one. Isaiah 55:1-2 invites the hungry and thirsty to come to God's provision, and Isaiah 49:10 promises that "they shall not hunger or thirst." Jesus applies this language to those who long for God's justice and righteous order.

"Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy" (v. 7). The correspondence is exact: mercy given, mercy received. This principle runs throughout Israel's scriptures. Proverbs 14:21: "Whoever is generous to the poor — blessed is he." The structure anticipates the parable of the unmerciful servant (18:23-35) and the judgment scene (25:31-46), where treatment of others determines how one is treated. In this author's larger argument, mercy is not optional for those who belong to the kingdom.

"Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (v. 8). Psalm 24:3-4 asks: "Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart." The "pure in heart" (katharoi te kardia) are those whose inner orientation is undivided, not duplicitous. The promise that they "shall see God" (ton theon opsontai) echoes the ultimate hope — in Psalm 17:15, "I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness." Access to God's presence belongs to those without inner corruption.

"Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God" (v. 9). The title "sons of God" (huioi theou) connects to the heavenly declaration at Jesus's baptism: "This is my beloved Son." Those who make peace bear the family resemblance — they are doing what God does. God is characterized throughout Israel's scriptures as the one who makes and offers peace (shalom). The peacemakers participate in God's own work and are therefore recognized as belonging to his family.

"Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (v. 10). This declaration forms an inclusio (a bracketing structure) with verse 3 — both end with "for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," and both use the present tense. The kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit and to the persecuted. The cause of the persecution matters: it is "for righteousness' sake" (heneken dikaiosynes). This is not suffering in general, but suffering that comes specifically because one is aligned with God's will. The author is already preparing the reader for the reality that following this king will produce opposition.

"Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account" (vv. 11-12). The shift from third person ("blessed are those who...") to second person ("blessed are you") is significant. Jesus now addresses his disciples directly. The persecution is now specified further: it is "on my account" (heneken emou). This is a remarkable claim. Jesus equates alignment with himself to alignment with righteousness (v. 10). To be persecuted because of him is the same as being persecuted for righteousness. The author places Jesus at the center of what it means to live rightly before God.

"Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you." The phrase "the prophets who were before you" (tous prophetas tous pro hymon) is extraordinary. Jesus places his disciples in the lineage of Israel's prophets. They are not merely followers of a teacher — they stand in the prophetic succession. And the history of Israel shows what happened to the prophets: Elijah was hunted, Jeremiah was imprisoned, Uriah was killed (Jeremiah 26:20-23), and tradition held that Isaiah was sawn in two. The pattern of persecution is not an aberration; it is the normal experience of those who speak and live for God within Israel's history.

div.title: Salt and Light: The Function of the Disciples (vv. 13-16)
div.p: Having described who is blessed in the kingdom, Jesus now describes what these people are for. He uses two metaphors.

"You are the salt of the earth" (v. 13). Salt in the first-century world served primarily as a preservative and as a flavoring agent. The image suggests that the disciples serve a preserving function in the world. But the warning is immediate: "If salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet." The word translated "lost its taste" (moranthe) is related to moros, meaning "foolish" — the same word that will appear in 7:26 (the "foolish" man who built on sand) and 25:2-3 (the "foolish" virgins). Salt that has become moranthe has become foolish, useless, good for nothing. The warning is that the disciples' distinctive character can be lost, and if lost, it cannot be recovered. They are not automatically preserved in their role; their saltiness — their distinctive identity as kingdom people — must be maintained.

"You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden" (v. 14). Isaiah 42:6 describes the Servant as "a light for the nations" (phos ethnon), and Isaiah 49:6 repeats the same phrase. Jesus transfers this vocation to his disciples: they are now the light of the world. The "city set on a hill" echoes Isaiah 2:2-3, where the mountain of the LORD's house is established as the highest of mountains, and all nations stream to it. The disciples collectively form this visible city. The point is visibility — the kingdom community cannot and should not be hidden.

"Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven" (v. 16). The "good works" (kala erga) are the visible expression of kingdom life. The purpose is not that the disciples receive praise, but that onlookers "give glory to your Father who is in heaven." This connects to the author's consistent emphasis on God as Father — a designation that will pervade the entire discourse (5:16, 45, 48; 6:1, 4, 6, 8, 9, 14, 15, 18, 26, 32; 7:11, 21). The audience's relationship to God is characterized as a father-child relationship, and the goal of their visible conduct is to bring honor to the Father.

div.title: Jesus and the Torah: Fulfillment, Not Abolition (vv. 17-20)
div.p: This section is the interpretive key to everything that follows in the discourse and, in many respects, to the entire document.

"Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them" (v. 17). The word "fulfill" (plerosai) is the same word used in 3:15 ("to fulfill all righteousness") and throughout chapters 1-2 for prophetic fulfillment (1:22, 2:15, 2:17, 2:23). The author's consistent usage of this word means "to bring to full expression, to complete, to fill up the measure of." Jesus is not setting aside the Torah and the Prophets. He is bringing them to their intended fullness.

This is critical for understanding what follows. The six contrasts in verses 21-48 ("You have heard that it was said... but I say to you") are not corrections of Moses. They are demonstrations of what the Torah looks like when it is filled to its full measure, brought to the depth and completeness that was always its trajectory.

"For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished" (v. 18). An "iota" (iota) corresponds to yod, the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet. A "dot" (keraia) refers to the tiny decorative strokes or projections that distinguish similar Hebrew letters from one another. Jesus affirms the permanence of the Torah down to its smallest features. The phrase "until all is accomplished" (heos an panta genetai) indicates that the Torah remains in force throughout the period of accomplishment — it does not expire but is brought to completion.

"Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven" (v. 19). The verb "relaxes" (lyse) means to loosen, undo, or annul. The one who undoes even the smallest commandment and teaches others to do so is "least" in the kingdom. The one who practices and teaches them is "great." The standard is both doing and teaching — practice and instruction together.

"For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven" (v. 20). This verse is the thesis statement for everything that follows. "Righteousness" (dikaiosyne) again — the same word from 3:15, 5:6, and 5:10. The scribes were the professional interpreters of the Torah; the Pharisees were the movement most committed to careful Torah observance. To a first-century Jewish audience, saying that their righteousness must exceed (perisseuse pleion) that of the scribes and Pharisees would have been staggering. If the most observant people in Israel are the benchmark, and you must surpass them, what could that possibly look like?

The six contrasts that follow (vv. 21-48) answer precisely that question. They show what "exceeding" righteousness looks like. It is not less Torah but more — not the letter only but the full depth of what the Torah was always driving at.

div.title: First Contrast: Killing and Anger (vv. 21-26)
div.p: "You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment'" (v. 21). The commandment is from Exodus 20:13 / Deuteronomy 5:17. "Those of old" (tois archaiois) refers to the generation that received the Torah at Sinai.

"But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment" (v. 22). Jesus extends the commandment from the act to the inner disposition that produces the act. Anger (orgizomenos) toward a brother places one under the same liability as murder. The progression intensifies: calling someone "Raka" (an Aramaic term of contempt, roughly "empty-headed") makes one liable to the council (synedrion); calling someone "fool" (more) makes one liable to the gehenna of fire. Gehenna (geenna) refers to the Valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom) outside Jerusalem, where according to 2 Kings 23:10, children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech. By Jeremiah's time (Jeremiah 7:31-32), it had become a symbol of God's judgment. In first-century usage, it functioned as shorthand for the place or state of final destruction.

The logic is not that words are literally equivalent to murder in a legal sense. The logic is that the Torah's prohibition of murder was always aimed at protecting the dignity and life of the neighbor, and that anger and contempt violate the same principle at its root. A righteousness that exceeds the scribes' does not merely avoid killing — it roots out the hostility that makes killing conceivable.

Verses 23-26 provide two practical illustrations. First, if you are bringing your gift to the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave the gift, go be reconciled, then come back and offer it. The priority is clear: reconciliation takes precedence over worship. The Temple offering is not refused, but it must wait until the horizontal relationship is repaired. Second, settle with your accuser quickly while you are on the way to court, lest you be handed to the judge and thrown into prison. "You will never get out until you have paid the last penny" (kodranten, a Roman coin of very small value). The urgency is real: unresolved conflict leads to outcomes that cannot be easily reversed.

div.title: Second Contrast: Adultery and Desire (vv. 27-30)
div.p: "You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery'" (v. 27). From Exodus 20:14 / Deuteronomy 5:18.

"But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (v. 28). Again, Jesus moves from the external act to the internal disposition. The phrase "in his heart" (en te kardia autou) locates the transgression internally. The tenth commandment already prohibited coveting a neighbor's wife (Exodus 20:17), so this is not entirely without Torah precedent — Jesus is drawing out what was already implicit. The heart, in the author's usage and in the broader scriptural tradition, is the seat of the will and intention, not merely of emotion. What the heart generates matters to God, not only what the body performs.

Verses 29-30 use hyperbolic language about plucking out an eye or cutting off a hand. "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into gehenna." The hyperbole drives home the seriousness: whatever leads to sin must be dealt with radically. The author is not prescribing self-mutilation (a literal reading would be absurd, since the left eye could still look lustfully). The point is that no cost is too high to avoid the destruction of the whole self.

div.title: Third Contrast: Divorce (vv. 31-32)
div.p: "It was also said, 'Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce'" (v. 31). This refers to Deuteronomy 24:1-4, which Moses permitted. The author will return to this topic at greater length in Matthew 19:3-9, where Jesus explicitly states that Moses permitted divorce "because of your hardness of heart, but from the beginning it was not so."

"But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery" (v. 32). The exception clause "except on the ground of sexual immorality" (parektos logou porneias) uses porneia, a broad term covering various forms of sexual transgression. This is the author's unique contribution among similar passages in the other accounts. The logic is that marriage creates a bond that divorce does not actually sever in God's eyes; therefore, a subsequent marriage constitutes adultery. The exception for porneia acknowledges a situation where the bond has already been violated.

The pattern continues: Jesus does not dismiss the Torah's provision but drives past it to the deeper principle that the Torah was accommodating. The Deuteronomy provision was a concession to human hardness; Jesus points to the original divine intention.

div.title: Fourth Contrast: Oaths (vv. 33-37)
div.p: "Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn'" (v. 33). This draws on Leviticus 19:12 ("You shall not swear by my name falsely") and Numbers 30:2 ("When a man vows a vow to the LORD... he shall not break his word").

"But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all" (v. 34). Jesus prohibits swearing by heaven ("it is the throne of God"), by the earth ("it is his footstool"), by Jerusalem ("it is the city of the great King"), or by one's own head ("you cannot make one hair white or black"). The reasoning is that all these things belong to God, and invoking them in an oath is attempting to leverage something one does not control.

"Let what you say be simply 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no.' Anything more than this comes from evil" (v. 37). The word "evil" (tou ponerou) could be translated "from the evil one" (the article suggests a personal referent) or "from evil" (the condition). The principle is radical simplicity and truthfulness: if your character is such that your yes means yes and your no means no, oaths become unnecessary. The need for oaths implies that ordinary speech cannot be trusted. Jesus demands a righteousness where ordinary speech is inherently trustworthy.

div.title: Fifth Contrast: Retaliation (vv. 38-42)
div.p: "You have heard that it was said, 'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth'" (v. 38). The lex talionis appears in Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20, and Deuteronomy 19:21. In its original context, it was not a command to retaliate but a limitation on retaliation — the punishment must not exceed the injury. It was a principle of proportional justice, replacing the escalating blood feuds common in the ancient world.

"But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil" (v. 39a). The verb "resist" (anthistemi) means to stand against, to oppose in kind — to meet force with equal and opposite force. Jesus does not prohibit defending the helpless or seeking justice (the context is personal retaliation). What follows is not passive submission but four concrete scenarios drawn from first-century life, each depicting a situation of structured inequality in which one party holds recognized power over the other. In each case, the prescribed response is an act that strips the powerful party of the mechanism by which they exercise dominance.

list.item: "If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also" (v. 39b). A slap on the right cheek, delivered by a right-handed person, would be a backhanded blow. In the first-century Mediterranean world, the backhand was not combat between equals. It was the gesture of a superior disciplining an inferior — master to slave, Roman to subject, patron to client. The social taxonomy of blows was precise: the Mishnah (Baba Qamma 8:6, codifying norms already operative in the period) assigned a fine for a backhanded slap double that of an open-handed blow, precisely because the backhand carried the additional injury of degradation. The inferior was expected to absorb it in silence — to accept the enacted hierarchy.

div.p: But if the struck person turns the left cheek, the aggressor's right hand cannot deliver another backhand. To strike the left cheek with the right hand requires either a fist or an open palm — both of which are blows exchanged between equals. The person who was struck has not retaliated, has not fled, and has not cowered. They have done something more disruptive: they have made it impossible for the aggressor to repeat the gesture of dominance without implicitly treating the inferior as a peer. The striker now faces a dilemma with no good exit — escalate to a fight between equals (thereby conceding the other's equal standing) or stop. The one who was slapped has seized the initiative without returning a blow.

list.item: "If anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well" (v. 40). The scenario is a courtroom: a creditor is suing a debtor for the inner garment (chiton). Only the truly destitute would have their clothing seized as collateral — Torah already recognized this and limited the practice. Exodus 22:26-27 and Deuteronomy 24:10-13 required that a cloak taken as a pledge be returned before sunset, because the poor person needed it for warmth. The creditor held all the legal power; the debtor stood exposed before the court's authority.

div.p: Jesus's instruction to surrender the outer garment (himation) as well would leave the debtor standing naked in court. In Jewish moral tradition, the shame of nakedness falls on the one who caused or witnessed it, not on the one exposed. This principle is foundational: in Genesis 9:20-27, Ham is cursed for seeing Noah's nakedness, while Shem and Japheth are blessed for covering it without looking. Habakkuk 2:15 pronounces woe on the one who strips his neighbor. Isaiah 20:1-4 uses nakedness as a sign of the shame brought upon nations by their oppressors. By stripping in the courtroom, the debtor transforms a private legal proceeding into a public spectacle that exposes the creditor's greed and the system's cruelty. The creditor, who entered the court holding legal power over the debtor, is now the one publicly shamed. The power dynamic has inverted without the debtor raising a hand.

list.item: "If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles" (v. 41). The verb "forces" (angareuo) is a technical term from Persian administration, adopted into Roman practice, for the legal right of a soldier to conscript a civilian to carry his pack for a prescribed distance. Roman military regulations governed and limited this impressment; unchecked requisitioning bred the kind of local resentment that destabilized occupied territories, and soldiers who abused the system could face disciplinary consequences. During the compulsory mile, the soldier holds all the power — he commands, the civilian obeys. The civilian is a tool, not a person.

div.p: But when the civilian voluntarily continues into the second mile, the entire dynamic shifts. The soldier, not the civilian, is now the one in an uncomfortable position: if an officer sees a civilian still carrying the pack beyond the permitted distance, it is the soldier who appears to have violated the regulations. The compeller becomes the one who is anxious. He may find himself in the absurd position of asking — even begging — the civilian to put the pack down. The one who was conscripted is now the one making choices; the one who conscripted him is now the one at risk. The civilian's voluntary act has turned Roman military power back on itself without any act of defiance.

list.item: "Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you" (v. 42). In the patronage networks that structured first-century Mediterranean society, lending and giving were not neutral acts of generosity. They were instruments of social power. A loan created obligation; a gift from a patron bound the client in a web of reciprocity and dependence. Proverbs 22:7 states the dynamic plainly: "The borrower is the slave of the lender." Deuteronomy 15:7-11 commands open-handed lending to the poor precisely because the natural calculation is to withhold and thereby maintain leverage. Jesus's instruction to give and lend without refusal — without the calculus of what will be returned or what obligation will be created — removes the mechanism by which generosity is converted into control. The giver retains no hold on the recipient. The transaction that normally reinforces hierarchy is emptied of its power to bind.

div.p: The pattern across all four cases is more precise than active generosity that exceeds what is demanded. Each example depicts a situation of structured inequality — social rank, economic power, military occupation, financial dependency — and in each case the prescribed response is an act that strips the powerful party of the specific mechanism by which they exercise control. The person in the inferior position does not retaliate (which would invite overwhelming force and leave the power structure unchallenged), nor merely comply (which would leave it intact and confirmed), but acts in a way that exposes the injustice and forces the oppressor into a dilemma they cannot resolve without conceding ground. This is what "exceeding" righteousness looks like in the face of real powerlessness — not acquiescence, not violence, but a creative refusal to cooperate with the terms of one's own domination.

div.title: Sixth Contrast: Love of Enemies (vv. 43-48)
div.p: "You have heard that it was said, 'You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy'" (v. 43). The first half is from Leviticus 19:18. The second half — "hate your enemy" — is not a Torah quotation. It may reflect a popular inference or an interpretation found in some communities (the Dead Sea Scrolls' Community Rule, 1QS 1:9-10, instructs members to "love all the sons of light... and hate all the sons of darkness"). Jesus addresses not just the written text but the interpretive tradition built around it.

"But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you" (v. 44). This is the climax of all six contrasts. Each one has pushed deeper into the intention behind the commandment, and this final one pushes furthest: love must extend even to those who are hostile to you. The word "love" (agapate) is a command — a verb in the imperative. This is not a feeling to cultivate but an action to perform. "Pray for those who persecute you" makes the action concrete: intercede before God on behalf of the very people who harm you.

"So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven" (v. 45). This clause reveals the logic. The reason for loving enemies is to resemble the Father. And the Father's character is demonstrated by observable action: "He makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust." God's provision is indiscriminate — he does not withhold rain from the wicked or sunshine from the unjust. His generosity is not conditioned on the moral status of the recipient. To be "sons of your Father" means to share this characteristic: acting benevolently toward all, not only toward those who deserve it.

"For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?" (v. 46). Tax collectors (telonai) were among the most despised figures in first-century Jewish society — collaborators with the Roman occupation who enriched themselves by overtaxing their own people. Even they love those who love them. Reciprocal love requires nothing distinctive.

"And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?" (v. 47). The comparison to Gentiles (ethnikoi) makes the same point: if your conduct is indistinguishable from those who do not know God, you are not yet living the kingdom's righteousness.

"You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect" (v. 48). The word "perfect" (teleioi) does not primarily mean flawless in the modern sense. It comes from telos, meaning end, goal, or completion. Teleios means complete, mature, having reached the intended goal. The LXX uses it in contexts of wholeness and integrity — being wholly devoted, not double-minded. In this context, after the command to love enemies, "perfect as your Father is perfect" means: be complete in your love the way God is complete in his love. God's love is not partial — it extends to the evil and the good alike. The disciples' love must also be whole, not restricted to those who reciprocate it.

This verse functions as the capstone of the entire chapter. The "exceeding" righteousness of verse 20 is now defined: it is a completeness that mirrors the Father's own character. Every contrast in verses 21-48 has been driving toward this conclusion. The Torah addressed external acts; Jesus drives to the interior disposition and extends the scope of obligation outward — not less law but fuller, deeper, more demanding compliance with the intention that was always embedded in the commands.

div.title: The Chapter's Function in the Author's Larger Argument

list.item: It defines the character of kingdom people. The declarations of blessedness (vv. 3-12) describe not what the disciples must become but who already stands in divine favor as the kingdom arrives: the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek, those longing for righteousness, the merciful, the pure, the peacemakers, and the persecuted. These are the ones the kingdom is for. This directly continues the theme from chapter 4, where Jesus proclaimed the kingdom's nearness and drew people to himself.

It establishes that kingdom identity carries a public function. Salt and light (vv. 13-16) are not decorative images. Salt that loses its character is discarded. Light that is hidden is pointless. The author presents the disciples as having a preserving and illuminating role in the world, and warns that this role can be lost. This connects to the author's developing theme that status without corresponding conduct is worthless — the same point John made about Abrahamic descent in chapter 3.

It positions Jesus's authority in relation to the Torah. The statement in verses 17-20 is foundational for the entire document. Jesus does not replace the Torah; he fills it to its fullest expression. The author will build on this throughout: Jesus's conflicts with the Pharisees will never be about abandoning Moses but about what Moses truly intended at the deepest level.

It demonstrates what "exceeding righteousness" looks like in practice. The six contrasts (vv. 21-48) show the pattern: the Torah commanded a minimum; Jesus reveals the maximum. Do not murder becomes do not harbor anger. Do not commit adultery becomes do not entertain lust. Proportional justice becomes radical non-retaliation. Love of neighbor becomes love of enemy. At every point, the trajectory is the same — deeper, wider, more complete conformity to the character of the Father.

It introduces "the Father" as the central relational category. God is referred to as "your Father" or "your heavenly Father" repeatedly in this chapter (vv. 16, 45, 48). This language will intensify dramatically in chapter 6 (the prayer begins "Our Father"). The author is establishing that the relationship between the disciples and God is defined by intimate familial language, and that the disciples' conduct is to be governed by resemblance to their Father's character.

It connects "fruit" to the kingdom's demands. Although the word "fruit" does not appear in this chapter, the concept permeates it. John demanded "fruit worthy of repentance" in chapter 3. Here, Jesus specifies what that fruit looks like: reconciliation over anger, purity over lust, faithfulness over divorce, truthfulness over oaths, generosity over retaliation, love over hostility. The "good works" of verse 16 are this fruit made visible to the world.

div.title: Matthew 6 — First-Century Reading
Context Within the Author's Argument
div.p: What came before (Matthew 5): The author presented Jesus ascending a mountain, sitting down (the posture of a teacher with authority), and beginning extended instruction to his disciples with the crowds also present. Jesus opened with a series of declarations about who is blessed under God's reign — the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek, those hungering for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, peacemakers, and the persecuted. He then declared his hearers to be salt and light, stated that he came not to abolish the Torah and Prophets but to fulfill them, and warned that their righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. The remainder of chapter 5 provided six concrete examples of this exceeding righteousness, each following the pattern "You have heard that it was said... but I say to you," addressing murder/anger, adultery/lust, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and love of enemies. The chapter closed with the command "Be perfect (teleioi) as your heavenly Father is perfect" — a standard of wholeness modeled on God's own character.

What comes after (Matthew 7): The author continues the mountain instruction with warnings against judging others (7:1-5), a saying about giving what is holy to dogs (7:6), encouragement to ask, seek, and knock with confidence in the Father's generosity (7:7-11), the "golden rule" as a summary of the Torah and Prophets (7:12), and then a series of sharp warnings: the narrow gate versus the wide gate, false prophets known by their fruits, and the final parable of two builders — one who hears Jesus's words and does them (house on rock) versus one who hears and does not do them (house on sand). The Sermon concludes with the crowds' astonishment because Jesus taught "as one having authority, and not as their scribes."

How chapter 6 connects them: Chapter 5 established the principle of exceeding righteousness and illustrated it through six case studies drawn from the Torah. Chapter 6 shifts from Torah commandments to religious practices — almsgiving, prayer, and fasting — and then to the deeper question of what a person's life is oriented toward. Chapter 7 will conclude with the demand that hearing must become doing. The movement across all three chapters is coherent: chapter 5 redefines obedience to Torah, chapter 6 redefines religious devotion and material orientation, and chapter 7 warns that only actual performance of these teachings constitutes a secure foundation. The author's argument never leaves the question announced at 5:20: what does it look like for righteousness to exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees?

div.title: The Thesis Statement on Practiced Righteousness (v. 1)
div.p: The chapter opens: "Beware of practicing your righteousness (dikaiosynen) before people in order to be seen by them, for then you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven."

The word "righteousness" (dikaiosyne) here connects directly to the programmatic use the author has been building. Jesus's first words in this document were about fulfilling "all righteousness" (3:15). At 5:6, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are declared blessed. At 5:10, those persecuted for the sake of righteousness are blessed. At 5:20, the disciples' righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. Now at 6:1 the author specifies what "practicing righteousness" looks like in the domain of religious observance, and immediately identifies the danger: performing it "before people in order to be seen by them" (pros to theathenai autois).

The verb theathenai (to be seen, to be made a spectacle) shares its root with theatron (theater). The author is describing religious conduct performed as theater — staged for an audience. The warning is not against public visibility per se (Jesus has just told these same people in 5:16 to let their light shine before others so that people see their good works and glorify the Father). The distinction the author draws is in the purpose clause: "in order to be seen by them" versus "so that they may glorify your Father." The orientation of the act — toward human approval or toward the Father — determines its character.

The consequence is stated in economic terms: "you have no reward (misthon) from your Father who is in heaven." The word "reward" (misthos) will structure the entire section that follows. It appeared already at 5:12 ("your reward is great in heaven") and 5:46 ("what reward do you have?"). The author consistently uses misthos to describe the Father's response to conduct. It is not a payment for services but the Father's recognition and response. The issue in 6:1 is that those who perform for a human audience have already received what they were after — the human audience's approval — and have nothing further coming from the Father.

div.title: Three Parallel Examples: The Hidden-Versus-Public Pattern (vv. 2-18)
div.p: The author now presents three religious practices — giving to the needy, prayer, and fasting — in a carefully parallel structure. Each follows the same pattern:

list.item: "When you..." (the practice is assumed, not optional)
"Do not be like the hypocrites who..." (the negative example, performed publicly for human approval)
"Truly I say to you, they have received their reward" (apechousin ton misthon auton)
"But when you..." (the positive instruction, done in hiddenness)
"And your Father who sees in secret will reward you" (the Father's response to what is hidden)

div.p: The repetition is deliberate and didactic. The author builds meaning through the threefold iteration.
div.title: Giving to the Needy (vv. 2-4)
div.p: "When you give alms" (hotan oun poies eleemosynen) — the "when," not "if," assumes the practice as a given for those under God's reign. Almsgiving (eleemosyne) was a core religious obligation in Second Temple Judaism. Tobit 4:7-11 presents it as laying up treasure for the day of necessity. Sirach 3:30 says almsgiving atones for sin as water extinguishes fire. The practice is not questioned; the manner is.

"Do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets." Whether a literal trumpet was ever sounded before almsgiving or this is hyperbolic imagery, the point is the same: orchestrating attention around one's generosity. The word "hypocrites" (hypokritai) comes from the Greek stage — a hypokrites was an actor, one who played a part behind a mask. The author's choice of this word reinforces the theater imagery from verse 1. These people are performing a role; their piety is a dramatic production.

"Truly I say to you, they have received their reward" (apechousin ton misthon auton). The verb apecho is a commercial term found on papyrus receipts meaning "paid in full." It appears in this technical sense in commercial documents of the period. The author uses it to say: the transaction is complete. They wanted human admiration; they got it. The account is settled. There is nothing further owed.

The counterinstruction: "Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing." This is vivid overstatement — one's own hands cannot "know" anything. The point is that secrecy should be so thorough that even the giver does not self-consciously observe the act. The giving should be so natural, so oriented toward the recipient and the Father, that the giver barely registers it as an achievement.

"Your Father who sees in secret (ho pater sou ho blepon en to krypto) will reward you." The "seeing" of the Father is set against the "being seen" by people. Both acts of giving are visible to someone. The question is which audience the giver plays to. The Father's seeing is described as active — he is watching precisely what is hidden from human eyes.
div.title: Prayer (vv. 5-15)
div.p: The prayer section is the longest of the three and contains the model prayer that the author presents as Jesus's instruction on how to pray.

The negative example (vv. 5-6): The hypocrites "love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, so that they may be seen by others." Standing was a normal posture for Jewish prayer (1 Samuel 1:26, 1 Kings 8:22), so the issue is not the posture but the location and motive — choosing conspicuous places for the sake of visibility. Again: "they have received their reward" (apechousin).

The positive instruction: "Go into your room (tameion) and shut your door and pray to your Father who is in secret." The tameion is an inner room or storage room — the most private space in a typical house. The shut door eliminates the audience. Prayer becomes a direct encounter between the person and the Father, with no third party to impress. The author's consistent emphasis is that the Father relates to what is genuine, not performed.

Against empty repetition (vv. 7-8): The author adds a second negative example, this time not from the hypocrites but from "the Gentiles" (ethnikoi). "Do not heap up empty phrases (battalogeo) as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard because of their many words." The verb battalogeo suggests babbling, stacking up repetitious syllables. The reference to Gentile practice points to pagan prayer customs that used lengthy invocations and repetitions of divine names to ensure the deity's attention (attested in Greco-Roman magical papyri and religious practice).

The reason this is unnecessary: "Your Father knows what you need before you ask him." This sentence redefines the purpose of prayer. If the Father already knows, then prayer is not about informing God or securing his attention through persistence or technique. Prayer is about the relationship between the one praying and the Father — about alignment, trust, and orientation of the will.
div.title: The Model Prayer (vv. 9-13)
div.p: "Pray then like this" (houtos oun proseuchesthe hymeis) — the "you" is emphatic (hymeis), contrasting with how the hypocrites and Gentiles pray. The prayer that follows is structured in two halves: three petitions oriented toward God (vv. 9-10) and three oriented toward human need (vv. 11-13).

"Our Father who is in heaven" (Pater hemon ho en tois ouranois): The address is corporate — "our," not "my." The one praying joins a community. The designation "Father" was not unknown in Jewish prayer (Isaiah 63:16, "You, O LORD, are our Father"; 64:8, "O LORD, you are our Father"), but its placement as the primary form of address in regular prayer is distinctive. The phrase "who is in heaven" locates the Father's authority beyond all earthly power — this is the one whose kingdom is being invoked.

"Hallowed be your name" (hagiastheto to onoma sou): A passive petition — "let your name be hallowed" or "may your name be made holy." In Ezekiel 36:23, God declares: "I will vindicate the holiness of my great name, which has been profaned among the nations." The hallowing of God's name in Ezekiel is something God himself does by acting in history to restore Israel and demonstrate his character before the nations. The petition asks God to act in such a way that his name — his revealed character and reputation — is recognized as holy.

"Your kingdom come" (eltheto he basileia sou): The kingdom (basileia) that John announced as "drawn near" (3:2) and Jesus proclaimed as "drawn near" (4:17) is here the subject of a petition. The fact that it can be prayed for indicates it has not yet fully arrived. The petition asks for its coming — its full establishment. In the context of first-century Judaism, this evokes the hope expressed in the Kaddish prayer: "May he establish his kingdom in your lifetime and in your days." The kingdom is God's active reign asserting itself over all competing powers.

"Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (genetheto to thelema sou, hos en ourano kai epi ges): This petition parallels and expands the previous two. The hallowing of the name, the coming of the kingdom, and the doing of God's will are three ways of expressing the same hope: that what is true in heaven (where God's sovereignty is uncontested) would become true on earth (where it is currently resisted and obscured). The scope is earth — not just Israel, not just the individual, but the whole created order.

These first three petitions are entirely about God — his name, his kingdom, his will. The one praying subordinates all personal concerns to God's purposes. This directly embodies the principle Jesus will state at 6:33: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness."

"Give us this day our daily bread" (ton arton hemon ton epiousion dos hemin semeron): The adjective epiousios is rare and debated — it appears nowhere else in surviving Greek literature before this text. Possible meanings include "for the coming day," "necessary for existence," or "sufficient for the day." Whatever the precise nuance, the petition is for provision that is limited to the present — "this day" (semeron). The one praying does not ask for a stockpile but for enough. This directly anticipates the anxiety passage in vv. 25-34, where worry about tomorrow's provision is addressed. It also echoes Israel's manna experience in Exodus 16, where the people received bread sufficient for each day and were prohibited from hoarding (those who tried found it spoiled). The petition positions the one praying in the same posture as Israel in the wilderness: daily dependence on God's provision.

"And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (kai aphes hemin ta opheilemata hemon, hos kai hemeis aphekamen tois opheiletais hemon): The word "debts" (opheilemata) is the author's chosen term (Luke's parallel uses "sins," hamartias). The metaphor of sin as debt owed to God was well established in Jewish thought. The petition binds together two actions: the forgiveness requested from God and the forgiveness already extended by the one praying to others. The verb "have forgiven" (aphekamen) is in the aorist tense — it describes forgiveness already performed, not a future intention. The one praying claims to have already forgiven those who wronged them, and on that basis asks the Father for the same.

This is not presented as a transaction (I forgive, therefore God must forgive) but as a coherence (the one who seeks forgiveness from God must be the kind of person who extends forgiveness to others). The author underscores this so heavily that it is the only petition from the model prayer that receives its own commentary in vv. 14-15.

"And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one" (kai me eisenenkes hemas eis peirasmon, alla rhysai hemas apo tou ponerou): The word peirasmos can mean "testing" or "temptation" — a moment of crisis that reveals whether faith holds or breaks. The petition asks not to be brought into such a moment, or if brought there, to be rescued from "the evil one" (tou ponerou, which can also be rendered "evil" abstractly, but the article suggests a personal figure). The petition acknowledges human vulnerability. Even those who pray rightly, give rightly, and forgive rightly remain susceptible to catastrophic failure and need the Father's active protection.
div.title: The Author's Commentary on Forgiveness (vv. 14-15)
div.p: Immediately after the model prayer, the author records Jesus expanding on the forgiveness petition alone: "For if you forgive others their trespasses (paraptomata), your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses."

The shift from "debts" (opheilemata) in the prayer to "trespasses" (paraptomata, literally "fallings-beside," missteps) in the commentary shows the author treating these as equivalent terms. The conditional structure is stark and binary: forgiveness given results in forgiveness received; forgiveness withheld results in forgiveness withheld. There is no third option — no scenario in which the one who refuses to forgive others nevertheless receives forgiveness from the Father. The author places this as the single elaboration on the prayer, signaling its centrality to the argument. In the author's understanding, the vertical relationship with the Father and the horizontal relationships with others are inseparable. One cannot seek reconciliation with God while maintaining enmity with people.

This will recur in the author's narrative. At 18:21-35, Peter asks how many times he must forgive, and Jesus tells the parable of the unforgiving servant — a man forgiven an astronomical debt who then refuses to forgive a trivial one. That parable ends: "So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart." The warning in 6:14-15 is not softened or qualified later; it is reinforced and dramatized.
div.title: Fasting (vv. 16-18)
div.p: The third example follows the established pattern exactly. "When you fast" — again, the practice is assumed, not debated. The hypocrites "disfigure their faces" (aphanizousin ta prosopa auton) to make their fasting visible. The verb aphanizo means to make unrecognizable, to mar — they alter their appearance to broadcast their self-denial. Their reward is the same as before: received in full from their human audience.

The counterinstruction: anoint your head and wash your face, "so that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret." Normal grooming conceals the fast. The faster appears unchanged to others. The audience of one — the Father — is the only one who needs to see.

The three examples together establish a principle that governs the entire section: religious practice performed for human recognition has already been compensated; religious practice oriented toward the Father, done in hiddenness, receives the Father's own response. The repeated structure drives this into the hearer's memory.

div.title: Competing Treasuries and the Question of Orientation (vv. 19-24)
div.p: The author now shifts from specific religious practices to the broader question of what governs a person's life. The transition is organic: if the danger in vv. 2-18 was performing piety for human approval, the danger in vv. 19-24 is orienting one's entire existence toward material accumulation. Both are forms of misdirected loyalty.
div.title: Two Treasuries (vv. 19-21)
div.p: "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal."

The contrast is between two storage locations. Earthly treasure is vulnerable — the author names three agents of destruction: moth (which consumes fabric, the primary form of stored wealth in the ancient world alongside grain and metal), rust or corrosion (brosis, literally "eating," which attacks metal and stored goods), and thieves who "dig through" (dioryssousin, literally "dig through" the mud-brick walls of typical Palestinian houses). Heavenly treasure is invulnerable to all three.

The concluding statement, "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also," reverses what might be expected. It does not say the heart leads and the treasure follows. It says the treasure leads and the heart follows. The location of one's investment determines the location of one's deepest loyalty and attention. This is a diagnostic: if you want to know where someone's heart is, look at where they store their wealth.
div.title: The Eye as the Body's Lamp (vv. 22-23)
div.p: "The eye is the lamp of the body. So if your eye is healthy (haplous), your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad (poneros), your whole body will be full of darkness."

The word haplous is often translated "healthy" or "sound," but its primary meaning is "single" or "simple" — without duplicity, undivided. In Jewish usage, a "good eye" (ayin tovah) indicated generosity, while an "evil eye" (ayin ra'ah) indicated stinginess and envy (see Deuteronomy 15:9, "your eye be evil against your poor brother"; Proverbs 22:9, "a good eye will be blessed, for he gives bread to the poor"; Sirach 14:10, "an evil eye begrudges bread"). The author places this saying between the teaching on treasure and the teaching on two masters, which strongly suggests the "single eye" refers to undivided loyalty and generosity, while the "evil eye" refers to divided, grasping orientation.

The metaphor works on two levels. Physically, the eye lets light into the body — if it functions well, the person can see and navigate; if not, they are in darkness. Morally, the way one "sees" — whether with generosity or with grasping — determines whether one's entire life is illuminated by God's purposes or plunged into darkness. The concluding warning sharpens the stakes: "If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!" If the very faculty by which one is supposed to perceive truth has become corrupted, there is no remaining source of guidance. Self-deception about one's own orientation is the deepest darkness.
div.title: Two Masters (v. 24)
div.p: "No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon."

The word "serve" (douleuein) means to be a slave to, not merely to work for. A slave in the first-century world was wholly owned — the slave's time, labor, and loyalty belonged entirely to the master. The impossibility is structural, not merely difficult. One cannot be wholly owned by two owners simultaneously. The emotional language — hate, love, be devoted to, despise — describes the inevitable outcome of attempting divided loyalty: one allegiance will win, and the other will be resented.

"Mammon" (mamonas) is an Aramaic word meaning wealth or property. It appears in Jewish literature (1 Enoch 63:10 uses it in reference to trusting in riches). By naming it alongside God as a competing master, the author personifies wealth as an alternative deity demanding total allegiance. The claim is not that money is inherently evil but that it functions as a rival lord — it demands the kind of total orientation that only God should receive.

The three sayings in vv. 19-24 form a progression: (1) where you store reveals where your heart is; (2) how you see determines whether you walk in light or darkness; (3) the ultimate loyalty question is binary — God or mammon. There is no synthesis, no both/and. The author presents this as a forced choice.

div.title: The Argument Against Anxiety (vv. 25-34)
div.p: The word "therefore" (dia touto) at the beginning of verse 25 marks this section as a consequence of what precedes it. Because one cannot serve both God and mammon, and because treasures should be stored in heaven rather than on earth, "therefore" — do not be anxious about the material necessities of life.
div.title: The Command and Its Basis (v. 25)
div.p: "Do not be anxious (me merimnate) about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?"

The verb merimnao does not mean to plan or to provide but to be consumed with worry, to be divided in one's mind (the root is related to meris, "a part" — anxiety divides the mind into competing concerns). The argument is from the greater to the lesser: if God gave you life itself and a body itself, will he not also provide the food and clothing those require? The one who gave the greater gift can be trusted for the lesser.
div.title: Two Arguments from Creation (vv. 26-30)
div.p: The birds (v. 26): "Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?" The birds do not engage in agricultural labor — the three activities named (sowing, reaping, gathering into barns) represent the full agricultural cycle. Yet the Father sustains them. The argument is a fortiori (from the lesser to the greater): if God provides for creatures that do not farm, how much more will he provide for "you" — those he has just called to seek his kingdom? The phrase "your heavenly Father" (ho pater hymon ho ouranios) keeps the relationship in view. This is not an argument from deism (a distant God who set up a self-sustaining system) but from fatherhood (a Father who actively feeds his dependents).

The lilies (vv. 28-30): "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." Solomon represents the apex of Israelite wealth and splendor (1 Kings 10:4-7 describes the Queen of Sheba's astonishment at Solomon's glory). To say that a wildflower surpasses Solomon is to demolish the assumption that human effort at accumulation can match what God freely provides. The flowers are then identified as "the grass of the field, which today exists and tomorrow is thrown into the oven." They are ephemeral — alive today, fuel tomorrow. If God so lavishly adorns what is temporary and disposable, "will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith (oligopistoi)?"

The term oligopistoi ("little-faiths") is distinctive to this author in the gospels. It appears here, at 8:26, 14:31, 16:8, and 17:20. Each time, it describes not the absence of faith but an insufficient measure of it — a faith that is real but too small for the situation. The disciples are not unbelievers; they are under-believers. Their anxiety about provision reveals not that they reject God but that they do not yet trust him enough.
div.title: The Argument Against Futility (v. 27)
div.p: Inserted between the birds and the lilies: "And which of you by being anxious can add a single cubit (pechyn) to his lifespan?" The word pechys literally means a cubit (about 18 inches), which is an unusual measure for lifespan — it works better for height ("stature"), but the context of life and death concerns suggests lifespan. Either way, the point is that anxiety is not only unfaithful but also ineffective. It accomplishes nothing. Worry cannot extend life by even the smallest increment. The argument is pragmatic: anxiety does not work, so why indulge it?
div.title: What the Gentiles Seek (vv. 31-32)
div.p: "Do not be anxious, saying, 'What shall we eat?' or 'What shall we drink?' or 'What shall we wear?' For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all."

The reference to "Gentiles" (ethne) echoes the earlier mention at v. 7 (the Gentiles who heap up empty phrases in prayer). In both cases, Gentile behavior serves as the negative model — not because Gentiles are inherently worse but because those who do not know the Father naturally fixate on securing their own provision and getting the gods' attention through their own effort. Those who know the Father should behave differently precisely because they know he is already aware of their needs. The repetition of "your heavenly Father knows" (from v. 8 about prayer and v. 32 about provision) ties the two halves of the chapter together: the same Father who does not need to be informed by lengthy prayers also does not need to be supplemented by anxious accumulation.
div.title: The Positive Command: Seek First (v. 33)
div.p: "But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you."

This is the climactic sentence of the chapter and one of the most important in the author's entire document. Two key words converge: "kingdom" (basileia), which has been the central announcement since 3:2, and "righteousness" (dikaiosyne), which has been a governing concept since 3:15 and the subject of the thesis at 5:20 and 6:1.

The command is not to abandon material needs but to reorder priorities. "First" (proton) establishes a hierarchy: the kingdom and its righteousness come before all other concerns. "All these things" (tauta panta) — food, drink, clothing, the material necessities just discussed — "will be added" (prostethsetai). The passive voice implies God as the agent: God will add them. Material provision is not dismissed or spiritualized; it is promised as a consequence of right ordering. The one who prioritizes the kingdom does not go without; the Father ensures provision.

The phrase "his righteousness" ties back to the entire discourse. The righteousness the author has been describing — the exceeding righteousness of 5:20, the practiced righteousness of 6:1, the conduct that reflects the Father's character — is what is to be sought. The kingdom and its righteousness are not two separate things; the righteousness defines what life under the kingdom looks like.
div.title: One Day at a Time (v. 34)
div.p: "Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble."

The personification of tomorrow ("tomorrow will be anxious for itself") is rhetorical: each day brings its own difficulties, and to borrow tomorrow's troubles today is to double the burden without gaining any advantage. This echoes the model prayer's request for bread "this day" (v. 11) and the manna principle of Exodus 16 — provision is daily, and so should trust be.

div.title: The Chapter's Function in the Author's Larger Argument
div.p: Matthew 6 advances the author's case on several fronts:

list.item: It defines what exceeding righteousness looks like in religious practice. The thesis of 5:20 (your righteousness must exceed the scribes' and Pharisees') received its first illustrations in Torah interpretation (5:21-48). Chapter 6 extends it to the practices of piety: the problem with the scribes and Pharisees is not that they pray, fast, and give alms, but that they perform these acts for human recognition. Exceeding their righteousness means performing the same acts for the Father alone.

It establishes the Father's hidden seeing as the ground of religious life. Six times the author refers to the Father "seeing in secret" or "knowing" what is needed. The entire religious life described in this chapter is oriented toward a divine audience who perceives what is invisible to human observers. This reframes piety from public performance to private relationship.

It presents the choice between God and mammon as absolute. The author does not allow a compromise position. Treasure is stored either on earth or in heaven. The eye is either single or evil. A person serves either God or mammon. This binary framing is consistent with the author's wider pattern of total sorting (3:12, wheat and chaff; 7:13-14, two gates; 7:24-27, two builders; 13:47-50, good and bad fish; 25:31-46, sheep and goats).

It grounds the command against anxiety in the character of the Father. The argument is not stoic detachment or ascetic renunciation. It is trust in a Father who knows, sees, and provides. The entire chapter depends on the identity of God as Father — a term used seventeen times in this single chapter. If God is not this kind of Father, the entire argument collapses. The author stakes everything on this relationship.

It connects forgiveness to the possibility of being forgiven. The author singles out the forgiveness petition for special emphasis, making explicit that refusal to forgive others blocks the Father's forgiveness. This is not incidental to the chapter; it is structurally highlighted as the one element of the model prayer requiring elaboration. The vertical and horizontal dimensions of righteousness cannot be separated.

It introduces "seek first the kingdom" as the orienting command. If 5:20 stated the standard (exceeding righteousness) and 6:1 identified the danger (performance for human eyes), then 6:33 provides the positive directive: orient your entire life toward the kingdom and its righteousness, and trust the Father to handle the rest. This becomes the organizing principle for all that follows.

div.title: Matthew 7 — First-Century Reading
Context Within the Author's Argument
div.p: What came before (Matthew 6): The author continued the mountain discourse by shifting from Torah reinterpretation (chapter 5) to religious practice and material orientation. Three parallel examples — almsgiving, prayer, and fasting — demonstrated that religious acts performed for human recognition have already received their full payment (apechousin ton misthon auton), while acts done in hiddenness receive the Father's own response. The model prayer was introduced, and its forgiveness petition was singled out for elaboration: the one who refuses to forgive others will not be forgiven by the Father. The chapter then turned to the question of ultimate loyalty — two treasuries, the single versus evil eye, God versus mammon — and concluded with the argument against anxiety: because the Father knows what his children need and actively provides, they should "seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness" (6:33) and trust that material provision will follow.

What comes after (Matthew 8-9): The author transitions from discourse to narrative. Jesus descends the mountain and immediately performs a series of healings and mighty works: a leper cleansed, a centurion's servant healed, Peter's mother-in-law restored, a storm stilled, demoniacs freed, a paralytic forgiven and healed, and more. The author presents these actions as demonstrations of the authority that the crowds recognized at 7:28-29. The one who taught "as one having authority" now acts with that same authority over disease, nature, demons, and sin. The transition from words to deeds is deliberate: chapters 5-7 established what Jesus teaches, and chapters 8-9 establish what Jesus does, and the author treats both as expressions of the same kingdom authority.

How chapter 7 connects them: Chapter 5 redefined obedience to Torah through six antitheses. Chapter 6 redefined religious devotion and material orientation. Chapter 7 now brings the entire discourse to its conclusion with a series of warnings and a final demand: hearing must become doing. The chapter moves from the interpersonal (how to relate to others regarding their faults, vv. 1-5), to confidence in the Father's generosity (vv. 7-11), to a summary principle (v. 12), and then into a sequence of sharp binary warnings — two gates, two trees, two claims of allegiance, two builders — all of which sort people into two categories based on whether they act on what they have heard. The author's argument never leaves the question raised at 5:20: what does it mean for righteousness to exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees? Chapter 7 answers: it means actually doing what Jesus has commanded, not merely hearing, affirming, or performing.

div.title: The Warning Against Judging (vv. 1-5)
div.p: "Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you."

The verb "judge" (krinete) in this context does not refer to all acts of evaluation or discernment — the chapter itself will demand discernment about false prophets (v. 15), about dogs and swine (v. 6), and about the fruit that reveals a person's true character (vv. 16-20). The prohibition targets a specific posture: setting oneself up as the pronouncer of verdict over another person. The structure reveals this. The one who judges places himself in the position of authority over another, but the author's Jesus warns that this act triggers a reciprocal process — the standard employed against others will be turned back on the one who employed it.

The phrase "with the measure you use it will be measured to you" (en ho metro metreite metrethsetai hymin) was a well-known principle in Jewish teaching. It appears in the Mishnah (Sotah 1:7): "By the measure with which a man measures, it is measured to him." The passive "will be measured to you" (metrethsetai) is a divine passive — God is the one who will apply the same standard. The warning is that the person who appoints himself judge of others has thereby established the standard by which God will judge him. If that standard is harsh, unsparing, and focused on fault-finding, that is the standard under which the judge himself will stand.

This connects directly to the forgiveness principle established at 6:14-15. There, refusal to forgive others resulted in the Father's refusal to forgive. Here, the principle is generalized: whatever measure one applies to others is the measure one will receive. The horizontal and vertical dimensions remain inseparable. The way one treats others determines how one is treated by God.
div.title: The Beam and the Splinter (vv. 3-5)
div.p: "Why do you see the speck (karphos) that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam (dokon) that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, 'Let me take the speck out of your eye,' when there is the beam in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye."

The karphos is a tiny fragment — a splinter, a bit of straw or chaff. The dokos is a massive construction timber, a roof beam. The disproportion is absurd and deliberately comic. The person with a roof beam protruding from his own eye offers to perform delicate surgery on someone else's splinter. The image exposes the self-deception inherent in the judgmental posture: the one most eager to identify faults in others is typically the one least aware of his own far greater faults.

The word "hypocrite" (hypokrita) returns. It was the controlling term in 6:2, 5, 16, where it described those who performed piety as theater. Here the same word applies to a different kind of performance: the person who stages moral authority over others while ignoring his own condition. The theatrical metaphor holds — this person is playing the role of righteous judge while being disqualified by his own failures.

Critically, the passage does not end by prohibiting all correction. It ends: "first take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye." The word "then" (tote) permits and even expects that after self-examination and self-correction, one may help a brother with his fault. The prohibition is not against mutual care within the community but against the arrogant presumption of judging others while exempt from scrutiny oneself. The sequence matters: self-examination first, then service to others.

The word "brother" (adelphos) appears twice. This is not about evaluating strangers or enemies but about conduct within the community of disciples. The warning is addressed to those within the circle of followers about how they treat one another.

div.title: The Saying About What Is Holy (v. 6)
div.p: "Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you."

This verse arrives without explicit transition and has often been read as disconnected from its context. But the author's method throughout this discourse has been to present complementary tensions, and this saying balances the preceding prohibition against judging. If vv. 1-5 warned against harsh, hypocritical evaluation of others, v. 6 warns against the opposite error: indiscriminate distribution of what is valuable without any evaluation at all. The two together establish a range: do not set yourself up as condemning judge, but do not abandon discernment entirely.

"Dogs" (kynes) and "swine" (choiroi) were both unclean animals in Israel's purity system (Leviticus 11:7 for swine; dogs were scavengers, associated with impurity in passages like 1 Kings 21:19 and Psalm 22:16). Both terms were used in Jewish discourse to refer to those outside the covenant who were hostile to Israel's holy things. "What is holy" (to hagion) likely refers to sacred teaching or sacred things — in later rabbinic usage, it was applied to sacrificial meat that must not be fed to dogs. "Pearls" (margaritas) represent what is precious and costly.

The warning is practical: some recipients will not merely ignore what is offered but will respond with contempt and violence — "trample them underfoot and turn to attack you." The author is not contradicting the command to love enemies (5:44) but recognizing that discernment is required in determining when and how to share what is sacred. The community of disciples needs judgment — not the condemning kind prohibited in vv. 1-2, but the discerning kind that recognizes when teaching will be received and when it will provoke destruction.

div.title: Confidence in the Father's Generosity (vv. 7-11)
div.p: "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened."

The three imperatives — ask (aiteite), seek (zeteite), knock (krouete) — are all present tense, indicating continuous or habitual action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. The three passive constructions that follow — "it will be given," "you will find," "it will be opened" — are divine passives: God is the one who gives, who allows finding, who opens. The repetition in verse 8 restates the promise in universal terms: "everyone" (pas) who asks, seeks, knocks receives a response.

This passage follows naturally from 6:25-34, where the Father was presented as the one who knows what his children need before they ask. It also connects to the model prayer of 6:9-13, where the disciples were taught to bring their needs to the Father directly. If the Father already knows (6:8, 32) and already provides (6:26, 30), why ask? Because prayer, as the author has presented it, is not about informing God but about the posture of dependence. The act of asking expresses trust. The act of seeking expresses desire for the kingdom. The act of knocking expresses persistent confidence that the door will open. The command to ask is a command to maintain the orientation established at 6:33 — seeking first the kingdom.
div.title: The Father's Character as Guarantee (vv. 9-11)
div.p: "Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you then, who are evil (poneroi ontes), know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!"

The argument is again a fortiori — from the lesser to the greater. Human fathers, despite being "evil" (poneros, the same word used for the "evil eye" in 6:23 and "the evil one" in 6:13), possess enough natural affection to respond appropriately to their children's requests. A stone resembles a round loaf of bread; a serpent resembles a fish. The point is that even flawed human fathers do not mock their children by offering a dangerous or worthless counterfeit in place of what was requested.

The concession "you who are evil" is striking. Jesus does not soften or qualify this assessment of human moral condition. Even those who are his disciples, even those being taught to pray "Our Father," are described as poneros. The argument's force depends on the gap between human evil and divine goodness: if even evil people give good gifts to their children, "how much more" (poso mallon) will the Father — who is not evil, who is wholly good — give good things to those who ask?

The word "good things" (agatha) is unspecified. The author does not limit what the Father gives to material provision (though that was the subject in 6:25-34). In the context of the discourse as a whole, the "good things" would include everything the disciples have been taught to seek: the kingdom, righteousness, forgiveness, deliverance from evil, daily bread. The Father's giving is characterized by its generosity and appropriateness — he gives what is genuinely good, not counterfeit substitutes.

div.title: The Summary Principle (v. 12)
div.p: "So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Torah and the Prophets."

The word "so" (oun, "therefore") connects this saying to everything that has preceded it. It is not an isolated ethical maxim but a conclusion drawn from the discourse's argument. The logic runs: because the Father is generous to those who ask (vv. 7-11), and because the Father measures to you as you measure to others (vv. 1-2), and because forgiveness given is forgiveness received (6:14-15), therefore treat others as you wish to be treated.

The formulation is positive: "whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them." This is not merely the avoidance of harm (which would be the negative form, attested in Tobit 4:15: "What you hate, do not do to anyone") but the active pursuit of the other's good. The positive form is more demanding. Refraining from stealing is the negative; providing for someone's need is the positive. The author's Jesus requires the active form.

The concluding phrase, "this is the Torah and the Prophets" (houtos gar estin ho nomos kai hoi prophetai), is the second bookend of a frame the author opened at 5:17: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Torah or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them." At 5:17, Jesus declared his continuity with Torah and Prophets. Now at 7:12, he provides the summary of what Torah and Prophets demand. The entire discourse between these two statements — all the antitheses, all the instructions on piety, all the teaching on anxiety and treasure and prayer — is an exposition of what the Torah and Prophets actually require. And its essence is this: treat others as you would want to be treated.

This is consistent with how other first-century Jewish teachers summarized the Torah. The Talmud records that when Hillel was asked to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot, he replied: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn" (Shabbat 31a). Jesus's positive formulation goes beyond Hillel's negative one, but both share the conviction that the Torah can be distilled to a relational principle. The author places this summary at the pivot point of the chapter, marking the transition from instruction to warning.

div.title: The Two Gates and Two Roads (vv. 13-14)
div.p: "Enter through the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the road is broad that leads to destruction, and those who enter through it are many. For the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few."

The author now shifts from instruction to a series of four binary warnings, each dividing hearers into two groups. This is the first. The images are spatial: two gates and two roads. One gate is wide (plateia), its road broad (eurychoros), and it leads to destruction (apoleian). The other gate is narrow (stene), its road compressed or afflicted (tethlimmene, from thlibo, "to press, to afflict" — the same root as thlipsis, "tribulation"), and it leads to life (zoen).

The word tethlimmene deserves attention. The road that leads to life is not merely narrow in a spatial sense but is characterized by pressure and affliction. This connects to the declarations of blessedness in 5:10-12, where persecution for righteousness' sake was identified as the condition of those who belong to the kingdom. The road to life is hard precisely because the conduct Jesus has been describing — turning the other cheek, loving enemies, giving without recognition, forgiving those who wrong you, refusing to serve mammon — brings pressure and opposition from the world that operates on contrary principles.

The sorting is stark: "many" (polloi) enter through the wide gate; "few" (oligoi) find the narrow one.
