How chapter 20 connects them: Chapter 19 ended with Jesus's promise of reward to those who sacrifice everything for his name, followed immediately by the first-last reversal statement (19:30). Chapter 21 will present Jesus entering Jerusalem as the humble king who overturns expectations about what power looks like. Chapter 20 is the bridge between these two movements. It opens with a parable that dramatizes the 19:30 reversal — the vineyard laborers who worked all day receive the same as those who worked one hour, and the first-last saying is repeated at 20:16, forming an inclusio with 19:30 that brackets the parable as its illustration. Peter's question ("what will there be for us?") assumed a proportional reward system: more sacrifice yields more reward. The parable dismantles that assumption. The chapter then presents the third and most detailed passion prediction (20:17-19), which is immediately followed by the mother of Zebedee's sons requesting positions of honor for James and John — a request that reveals the disciples still think in terms of rank and reward even after hearing Jesus describe his coming death. Jesus responds with the servant-leadership teaching (20:25-28), which defines greatness as service and the Son of Man's own mission as giving "his life as a ransom for many." The chapter closes with two blind men crying out for mercy and receiving it — men who were rebuked by the crowd but whom Jesus stopped for, healed, and who then followed him. The movement is coherent: from the dismantling of transactional reward (parable), through the announcement of sacrificial death (passion prediction), through the exposure and correction of status-seeking (Zebedee's sons), to the concrete demonstration of what the Son of Man's service looks like (healing the blind). Chapter 20 prepares the reader for the Jerusalem entry by establishing what kind of king is arriving: one whose kingdom operates on generosity rather than merit, whose greatness is measured by service, and whose mission is to give his life.

div.title: The Vineyard Laborers and the Landowner's Generosity (vv. 1-16)
div.p: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner (oikodespotes) who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard."

The word "For" (gar) at the opening of 20:1 is critical. It is a conjunction of explanation — it connects what follows to what precedes. The parable does not begin a new topic; it illustrates the principle just stated at 19:30: "many who are first will be last; and the last, first." The gar tells the reader that the parable is the explanation of that reversal. Any reading of the parable that does not account for this connection to 19:30 severs it from the author's own stated purpose.

The image of the vineyard (ampelon) reaches deep into Israel's prophetic tradition. In Isaiah 5:1-7, the vineyard is Israel: "For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel" (Isaiah 5:7). In the LXX, the same vocabulary appears: ampelon kyriou Sabaoth oikos tou Israel. Jeremiah 12:10 uses the vineyard as an image of God's people, and Psalm 80:8-16 describes Israel as a vine God brought out of Egypt and planted. The author will use the vineyard image again in the parable of the wicked tenants (21:33-41), where it explicitly represents Israel and the tenants represent the faithless leaders. While the vineyard in 20:1-16 is not allegorized in the same way, a first-century Jewish hearer would have carried this association. The landowner (oikodespotes — master of the house) goes out personally to hire workers. This is not an absentee owner; he is directly and repeatedly engaged with the hiring.
"When he had agreed with the laborers for a denarius for the day, he sent them into his vineyard."

A denarius was the standard daily wage for a laborer (the same amount specified at 18:28, where the fellow servant owed "a hundred denarii," and confirmed by Tobit 5:15 and common Roman wage standards). The agreement (symphonesas — from symphoneo, to agree, to harmonize) is a formal contract. The first-hired laborers have a negotiated, agreed-upon wage. This detail is essential to the parable's logic: they have received exactly what they were promised.

"And he went out about the third hour and saw others standing idle in the marketplace; and to those he said, 'You go into the vineyard also, and whatever is right (dikaion), I will give you.' And so they went."

The third hour is approximately 9 a.m. (the workday began at dawn, roughly 6 a.m.). The marketplace (agora) was where day laborers gathered hoping for employment. Standing "idle" (argous — literally "without work," from a-ergos) is not laziness but unemployment. These are people willing to work who have not yet been hired. The landowner promises them "whatever is right" (ho ean e dikaion) — the word dikaios (just, righteous, right) signals that the payment will be fair but is not specified. These workers go to the vineyard on trust, without a fixed contract.
"Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour, and did the same thing."

The sixth hour (noon) and the ninth hour (3 p.m.) are progressively later in the day. Each time the landowner goes out personally. The repeated hiring underscores the owner's initiative: he is not passively accepting applicants but actively seeking workers.

"And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing around; and he said to them, 'Why have you been standing here idle all day long?' They said to him, 'Because no one hired us.' He said to them, 'You go into the vineyard too.'"

The eleventh hour is approximately 5 p.m. — one hour before the end of the workday. The laborers explain that their idleness is not refusal to work but exclusion from work: "no one hired us" (oudeis hemas emisthosato). They have been available all day; the fault is not theirs. The landowner sends them in with no promise of any specific amount. The progression from the first-hired (full day, specified wage) to the last-hired (one hour, no specified wage) sets up the reversal that follows.
"Now when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, 'Call the laborers and pay them their wages, starting with the last group to the first.'"

The payment instruction follows Torah. Leviticus 19:13 commands, "The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until morning," and Deuteronomy 24:15 requires, "You shall give him his wages on his day before the sun sets." The landowner is fulfilling the law's requirement of prompt payment. But the order is deliberate and unusual: "starting with the last group to the first" (arxamenos apo ton eschaton heos ton proton). This arrangement is necessary for the parable's dramatic structure — the first-hired must see what the last-hired receive before they receive their own payment. Without this reversal of payment order, the contrast would not be visible.

"When those hired about the eleventh hour came, each one received a denarius. And so when those hired first came, they thought that they would receive more; but each of them also received a denarius."

The last-hired receive a full day's wage for one hour of work. This is the hinge of the parable. The first-hired, seeing this, make a reasonable calculation: if those who worked one hour received a denarius, then surely those who worked twelve hours will receive twelve denarii, or at least significantly more. Their expectation follows the logic of proportional compensation — more work, more pay. The parable deliberately evokes this expectation so that it can be overturned. Each of the first-hired also receives a denarius — exactly what was agreed.

"When they received it, they grumbled (egongyzon) at the landowner, saying, 'These who were hired last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal (isous) to us who have borne the burden of the day's work and the scorching heat.'"

The verb gongyzo (to grumble, to murmur) has specific resonance in Israel's history. In the LXX, this is the verb used for Israel's grumbling against Moses and God in the wilderness. Exodus 16:7: "He has heard your grumbling (gongysmon) which you grumble against him" (speaking of the complaint about food). Numbers 14:27: "How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me? I have heard the grumblings of the people of Israel." The murmuring of Israel in the wilderness was a paradigmatic act of ingratitude — God had delivered them from Egypt, but they complained about the terms of the journey. The verbal echo places the first-hired laborers in the position of grumbling Israel: they received what was promised, but they resent the generosity shown to others.

The complaint focuses on equality: "you have made them equal to us" (isous autous hemin epoiesas). The objection is not that they were cheated — they received the agreed wage — but that others received the same without equivalent labor. The issue is comparison. The scorching heat (ton kausona) and burden of the day are real; their labor was genuine and demanding. The complaint has an internal logic of fairness. But it operates on the assumption that the landowner's resources should be distributed according to a merit-based proportion, and it is this assumption the parable challenges.

"But he answered and said to one of them, 'Friend (hetaire), I am doing you no wrong (ouk adiko se); did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go; but I want (thelo) to give to this last person the same as to you.'"

The address "Friend" (hetaire) is a word the author uses in very specific contexts. It appears only three times in this document: here (20:13), at 22:12 (where the king addresses the man without a wedding garment: "Friend, how did you get in here without wedding clothes?"), and at 26:50 (where Jesus addresses Judas in Gethsemane: "Friend, do what you have come for"). In each case, the word carries a note of formal distance — it is not the warm philos (beloved friend) but a cooler, more formal address. Each use precedes a confrontation or exposure. The landowner is not hostile, but he is correcting.

The defense is stated in legal terms: "I am doing you no wrong" (ouk adiko se). The verb adikeo (to wrong, to be unjust) puts the matter in the frame of justice. The laborer received what he agreed to. No contract was broken, no promise was violated. The landowner then states his will: "I want (thelo) to give to this last person the same as to you." The verb thelo (to will, to desire, to choose) is the same verb used in 19:21 ("if you want to be complete") and will appear prominently in the Gethsemane prayer (26:39, "not as I will, but as You will"). The landowner asserts his sovereign right to do with his own property as he wills. His generosity is not constrained by what the first-hired consider fair.
"Is it not lawful for me to do what I want with what is my own? Or is your eye envious (poneros) because I am generous (agathos)?"

The question "is it not lawful" (ouk exestin moi) uses the same phrase that appeared repeatedly in the Sabbath controversies (12:2, 10, 12). The landowner asserts his right (exousia) over his own possessions. The second question is literally "is your eye evil (poneros) because I am good (agathos)?" The "evil eye" (ophthalmos poneros) was a well-known Semitic idiom for envy, jealousy, and stinginess. In Deuteronomy 15:9, the Israelite is warned against having an "evil eye" (LXX: ophthalmos poneros) toward a poor brother when the sabbatical year approaches — grudging the release of debts. In Proverbs 23:6, "Do not eat the bread of a man who has an evil eye" (LXX: andros baskanou). Sirach 14:10: "An evil eye is grudging of bread." The evil eye is the eye that measures its own benefit against another's and resents another's good fortune. The landowner's "goodness" (agathos) echoes 19:17, where Jesus said, "There is only One who is good" — God. The contrast between the laborer's evil eye and the owner's goodness aligns the owner's character with divine generosity and exposes the laborer's complaint as a failure not of logic but of vision.
"So the last shall be first, and the first, last."

This repeats 19:30, completing the inclusio. The saying at 19:30 introduced the principle; the parable illustrated it; the saying at 20:16 seals it. The "first" (the first-hired, Peter and the disciples who gave up everything early, those who assume their seniority earns greater reward) become "last" because their transactional mindset puts them in opposition to the landowner's generosity. The "last" (the eleventh-hour workers, latecomers, those with no claim to merit) become "first" because they receive grace without the burden of comparison.

The parable's function in context is precise. Peter had just asked, "What will there be for us?" (19:27). Jesus answered generously — thrones, hundredfold return, eternal life (19:28-29). But then he immediately added the first-last reversal and followed it with this parable. The parable does not deny that there is reward for sacrifice; it denies that the reward operates on a proportional, merit-based system where those who sacrificed more receive more than those who sacrificed less. The kingdom operates on the landowner's generosity (agathos), not on the laborer's calculation. Peter's question was the right question asked in the wrong spirit — and the parable corrects the spirit while affirming the promise. Those who gave up everything will receive eternal life, but so will those who came to the vineyard at the eleventh hour, and the first-comers have no ground for complaint because they received exactly what was promised. The grievance arises only from comparison, and comparison is the evil eye that cannot see the owner's goodness.

div.title: The Third Passion Prediction (vv. 17-19)
div.p: "As Jesus was about to go up to Jerusalem, He took the twelve disciples aside by themselves, and on the road He said to them, 'Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn Him to death, and they will hand Him over to the Gentiles to mock and flog and crucify, and on the third day He will be raised up.'"

This is the third passion prediction in the document, following 16:21 and 17:22-23. Each prediction has been more specific than the last. The first (16:21) stated that Jesus "must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised." The second (17:22-23) said, "The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and he will be raised on the third day." This third prediction adds details absent from the first two: the handing over to Gentiles, the specific forms of suffering (mocking, flogging, crucifixion), and the identification of the chief priests and scribes as the agents who will condemn him. The geographical marker — "going up to Jerusalem" — signals that the narrative is now moving toward its climax. The verb anabaino (to go up) is the standard term for ascending to Jerusalem, which sits on a hill, but it also carries connotations of ascent in a broader sense: this is the movement toward the fulfillment of everything the document has been building toward.

The placement of this prediction immediately after the vineyard parable is significant. The parable demonstrated that the kingdom does not operate on proportional merit; the passion prediction demonstrates what the king himself will undergo. The Son of Man who is the subject of the prediction is the same figure who will define greatness as service in vv. 25-28. The prediction functions as the factual basis for the servant-leadership teaching that follows: the Son of Man can define greatness as service because he himself is about to enact the ultimate service — giving his life.

The verb paradidomi (to hand over, to deliver up, to betray) appears twice: the Son of Man will be "handed over" (paradothesetai) to the chief priests and scribes, and they in turn will "hand him over" (paradosousin) to the Gentiles. This verb carries enormous weight throughout the document. It was used for John the Baptist being "delivered up" (4:12), for the handing over of disciples to councils and flogging (10:17, 19), and it will be the verb used for Judas's betrayal (26:15-16, 21, 23-25, 45-46, 48). The double use here — handed over by one group, then handed over again to another — emphasizes the chain of complicity. Israel's leaders will condemn; Rome's agents will execute. Both are implicated.

The response to this prediction is striking for what it does not include: the disciples do not react with grief (contrast 17:23, where they "were deeply grieved"), do not question, do not protest (contrast 16:22, where Peter rebuked Jesus). Instead, the very next verse presents a request for positions of honor. The author juxtaposes the prediction of death with the request for thrones without any buffer, forcing the reader to see the disconnection between what Jesus has just said and what the disciples are still thinking.

div.title: The Request of the Mother of Zebedee's Sons (vv. 20-23)
div.p: "Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to Jesus with her sons, bowing down and making a request of Him. And He said to her, 'What do you desire?' She said to Him, 'Say that in Your kingdom these two sons of mine shall sit, one at Your right, and one at Your left.'"

The word "Then" (tote) places this request immediately after the passion prediction. The positioning is deliberate. Jesus has just described his coming humiliation, condemnation, mocking, flogging, and crucifixion. The mother's response is to seek the two highest positions in his kingdom for her sons. The verb proskyneo (to bow down, to worship, to prostrate oneself) indicates a posture of supplication before a king — she approaches Jesus as one approaching a ruler to petition for favor. The request for positions "at your right and at your left" (ek dexion sou kai ex euonymon sou) seeks the two seats of greatest honor in a royal court. In Solomon's court, Bathsheba sat at the king's right hand (1 Kings 2:19). The right and left of the king were the positions of the chief advisors, the highest-ranking officials.

James and John are with their mother — the verb "came to Jesus with her sons" (meta ton huion autes) makes clear they are present and presumably complicit. The mother may be the spokeswoman, but the sons are the petitioners. Their presence will be confirmed in v. 22, where Jesus addresses "them" (autois), not her. The request reveals that despite three passion predictions, the teaching about children and humility (18:1-5), the warning about the first being last (19:30), and the parable that just dismantled proportional merit (20:1-16), the disciples still understand the kingdom as a political structure with positions of rank to be distributed. They are thinking of thrones (19:28 promised twelve thrones), and they want the best ones.
"But Jesus replied, 'You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?' They said to Him, 'We are able.'"

Jesus's response — "You do not know what you are asking" (ouk oidate ti aiteisthe) — is not a rebuke but a statement of fact. They literally do not understand what sitting at his right and left will mean. The "cup" (poterion) Jesus is about to drink is a loaded image from Israel's prophetic tradition. In the Hebrew scriptures, the cup is consistently an image of God's judgment and wrath. Isaiah 51:17: "Rouse yourself, rouse yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (to poterion tou thymou, LXX), who have drunk to the dregs the bowl, the cup of staggering." Jeremiah 25:15: "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it." Psalm 75:8: "For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs." Ezekiel 23:31-34 describes the cup of horror and desolation. The cup Jesus is about to drink is the cup of suffering described in the passion prediction he has just given. At Gethsemane, he will pray, "My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me" (26:39). The cup is not metaphorical glory but literal suffering.

The sons' answer — "We are able" (dynametha) — is confident and immediate. They think they are being tested for worthiness; they are actually being asked whether they can share in Jesus's suffering. The confidence is ironic: within the narrative, both will flee when Jesus is arrested (26:56). Yet Jesus does not contradict their claim.
"He said to them, 'My cup you shall drink; but to sit at My right and at My left is not Mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by My Father.'"

Jesus affirms that James and John will indeed drink his cup — that is, they will suffer. Historically, James was the first of the twelve to be martyred (Acts 12:2, killed by Herod Agrippa). The promise "my cup you shall drink" is a promise of suffering, not a promise of rank. But the positions of honor are "not mine to give" — they belong to the Father's sovereign arrangement. The verb hetoimazo (to prepare) indicates a decision already made by the Father, not one subject to petition or negotiation. Jesus does not deny that positions exist; he denies that they are his to distribute and that they can be obtained by asking. The Father prepares them, and the criteria for that preparation are not disclosed. This is consistent with the vineyard parable's assertion that the landowner does what he wills with what is his own (20:15).

div.title: The Indignation of the Ten and the Teaching on Servant-Leadership (vv. 24-28)
div.p: "And after hearing this, the other ten disciples became indignant (eganaktesan) with the two brothers."

The verb aganakteo (to be indignant, to be angry, to be vexed) appeared at 21:15 (the chief priests and scribes were indignant at the children's cries) and at 26:8 (the disciples were indignant at the "waste" of expensive ointment). The ten are not angry because the request was inappropriate; they are angry because James and John tried to get ahead of them. Their indignation reveals the same competitive impulse that drove the request. If the ten were free of status-seeking, they would not be indignant — they would recognize the request as misguided and let Jesus's correction stand. Their anger shows that all twelve share the same orientation: they all want the positions, and they resent that two of them tried to jump the queue.

"But Jesus called them to Himself and said, 'You know that the rulers of the Gentiles domineer over them (katakyrienousin auton), and those in high position exercise authority over them (katexousiazousin auton). It is not this way among you (ouch houtos estai en hymin).'"

The two verbs — katakyrieuo (to lord it over, to exercise dominion) and katexousiazo (to exercise authority over) — are both intensified by the prefix kata-, which adds a sense of "down upon." These are not neutral descriptions of governance but descriptions of domination. The rulers of the Gentiles (hoi archontes ton ethnon) press their authority downward onto those beneath them. Jesus describes this as the known reality — "you know" (oidate) — of how the world outside the community operates. Herod Antipas, the Roman prefect, the client kings and their courts — the disciples have lived under this system. They know what top-down authority looks like.

The declaration "it is not this way among you" (ouch houtos estai en hymin) uses the future indicative (estai — it shall be), which functions as both a command and a description of the kingdom's nature. The community is not to replicate the Gentile model. The contrast is not between good authority and bad authority but between two entirely different structures: authority-as-domination versus authority-as-service.
"But whoever wants to become prominent among you shall be your servant (diakonos), and whoever desires to be first among you shall be your slave (doulos)."

The word diakonos (servant, one who serves, one who waits at table) denotes a person who provides practical service to others — originally a table-server. The word doulos (slave, bond-servant) is even more extreme: a doulos has no rights, no autonomy, no independent status. The doulos belongs entirely to another. The progression from diakonos to doulos is a deliberate intensification: if you want prominence, become a servant; if you want to be first, become a slave. The vocabulary inverts every category of rank. In the Greco-Roman world, the diakonos and the doulos occupied the lowest rungs of the social order. Jesus places them at the top of the kingdom's hierarchy — but the hierarchy itself has been inverted so that the top is defined by the bottom.

This teaching does not eliminate the categories of "great" (megas) and "first" (protos). Jesus does not say, "There will be no greatness among you." He redefines what greatness consists of. Greatness remains; its content changes. The one who is great is the one who serves. The one who is first is the one who is enslaved to the needs of others. This is continuous with 18:1-4, where the greatest in the kingdom is the one who humbles himself like a child, and with 23:11-12, where Jesus will state: "The greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted."
"Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom (lytron) for many (anti pollon)."

The phrase "just as" (hosper) makes the Son of Man the paradigm of what he commands. He does not merely teach servant-leadership; he embodies it. The Son of Man — the figure from Daniel 7:13-14 who receives dominion and glory and a kingdom "that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him" — came not to receive that service but to give service. The reversal is breathtaking from a first-century perspective: the one who is entitled to be served by all nations has come to serve.

The word lytron (ransom) appears only here and in the parallel passage in Mark 10:45 in the entire New Testament. In the LXX, the lytron word-group is rooted in Israel's experience of redemption. The cognate verb lytroo is used for God's redemption of Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8, "the LORD redeemed you," elytrosen se kyrios; Deuteronomy 9:26; 13:5; 15:15; 24:18). The noun lytron refers to the price paid to redeem or release someone from bondage, obligation, or death. In Exodus 21:30, a lytron is the payment that redeems a man's life when his ox has killed someone. In Numbers 35:31-32, a lytron (ransom) is forbidden for a murderer — his life cannot be bought back. In Psalm 49:7-8 (LXX 48:8-9), "No man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life (lytrosin tes psyches autou), for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice." The psalm declares human ransom impossible; Jesus declares that the Son of Man's life is the ransom that the psalm said no human could pay.

The preposition anti (in place of, instead of, in exchange for) indicates substitution. The lytron is given anti pollon — "in place of many" or "in exchange for many." The "many" (pollon) echoes Isaiah 53:11-12 (LXX): "The righteous one, my servant, shall make many (pollous) to be accounted righteous... he bore the sin of many (pollon)." The Servant of Isaiah 53 bears suffering on behalf of the many. Jesus identifies his death with this Servant's work: his life given as the price that secures the release of the many. The ransom-language is concrete and transactional — a lytron is a payment that effects a release — but the author does not specify to whom the payment is made. The emphasis falls on the act itself (giving his life), the nature of the act (ransom/redemption), and the beneficiaries (the many).

This verse is the theological climax of the chapter and the capstone of the servant-leadership teaching. The Son of Man's example is not merely moral (he was humble, so you be humble too); it is constitutive (his service — specifically his death as a ransom — is the foundation upon which the community's existence depends). The disciples are called to serve because the Son of Man served; and his service was the giving of his life to secure their freedom.

div.title: Two Blind Men Receive Mercy Outside Jericho (vv. 29-34)
div.p: "As they were leaving Jericho, a large crowd followed Him. And two people who were blind, sitting by the road, hearing that Jesus was passing by, cried out, 'Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!'"

The geographical marker — leaving Jericho, heading toward Jerusalem — places this event on the final approach to the city where the passion will occur. Jericho is approximately fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem, and the road between them climbs steeply upward through the Judean wilderness. Jesus is on his way to the death he has just predicted.

The two blind men sit "by the road" (para ten hodon). They are marginal figures — physically unable to work, dependent on alms, positioned at the roadside where they can beg from travelers. Their blindness places them among the "little ones" and the powerless whom the document has been concerned with since chapter 18. They cannot see Jesus, but they hear that he is passing by, and they cry out.

Their cry — "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David" (kyrie, eleeson hemas, huios Dauid) — combines two significant elements. First, kyrie eleeson (Lord, have mercy) is a prayer for divine compassion. The verb eleeo (to have mercy) connects to the mercy-language that pervades the document: the Hosea 6:6 quotations (9:13, 12:7: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice"), the beatitude (5:7: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy"), the Canaanite woman's plea (15:22: "Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David"), and the unforgiving servant's failure to show mercy (18:33). Second, "Son of David" is a messianic title. In Israel's tradition, the Son of David was the expected king from David's line who would restore the kingdom. The blind men address Jesus with the royal title that the author established in the opening genealogy (1:1: "Jesus Christ, the son of David"). They recognize Jesus as the Davidic king — they see, in the deepest sense, what they cannot physically see.

The combination of their physical blindness with their correct identification of Jesus is pointed. The disciples, who can see, have just demonstrated spiritual blindness: they heard the passion prediction and responded with a request for positions of power. The blind men, who cannot see, respond with the right prayer (mercy) addressed to the right person (the Son of David). The pattern inverts expectations about who truly perceives.
"But the crowd sternly warned them to be quiet (epetimesen autois ho ochlos hina siopsousin); yet they cried out all the more, 'Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!'"

The verb epitimao (to rebuke, to warn sternly, to censure) is the same verb used when the disciples rebuked those bringing children to Jesus (19:13). The crowd plays the same role the disciples played — gatekeeping, trying to silence those whom they consider unworthy of Jesus's attention. The blind men are treated as an annoyance, a disruption. They are nobodies — blind beggars by the roadside — and the crowd considers their cries an imposition on an important person's time.

But the blind men persist. "They cried out all the more" (meizon ekraxan — literally, "they cried out greater"). Their persistence recalls the Canaanite woman at 15:22-28, who was also initially rebuffed (by the disciples, 15:23, and by Jesus's initial silence) and who persisted until she received what she sought. In both cases, the marginal person — the Gentile woman, the blind beggars — displays the faith that the insiders lack. The crowd tries to silence them; they raise their voices. The crowd says "be quiet"; they say "have mercy" louder. Their persistence is itself a form of faith — they will not be deterred by social pressure from seeking the one who can help them.
"And Jesus stopped (statheis) and called them and said, 'What do you want Me to do for you?' They said to Him, 'Lord, we want our eyes to be opened.'"

The verb histemi (to stand, to stop) indicates that Jesus halted the entire procession. The crowd heading toward Jerusalem, the disciples, the momentum of the narrative toward the passion — all of it pauses because two blind men cried out. This is the Son of Man who "did not come to be served but to serve" (v. 28) — and here the service is demonstrated. He does not delegate; he stops personally.

The question "What do you want Me to do for you?" (ti thelete poieso hymin) is nearly identical to the question Jesus asked the mother of Zebedee's sons: "What do you desire?" (ti theleis, v. 21). The verbal parallel is deliberate. The mother wanted thrones for her sons; the blind men want their eyes opened. The contrast between the two requests exposes what each petitioner actually understands about Jesus. The mother sought political favor; the blind men seek healing. The mother sought to advance her sons above others; the blind men seek to be made whole. The mother's request was rooted in the competitive logic of who sits where; the blind men's request is rooted in need.
"Moved with compassion (splagchnistheis), Jesus touched their eyes; and immediately they regained their sight and followed Him."

The verb splagchnizomai (to be moved with compassion) appears here for the last time in the document's narrative. It appeared at 9:36 (Jesus saw the crowds "harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd" and had compassion), 14:14 (he saw the great crowd and had compassion and healed their sick), 15:32 (he had compassion on the crowd that had been with him three days without food), and it was the key verb describing the king in the parable of the unforgiving servant (18:27: "moved with compassion, the master released him and forgave him the debt"). Each use describes a visceral, gut-level response to human need. That this is the verb's final narrative appearance, occurring on the road to Jerusalem just before the passion begins, is significant: the compassion that has characterized Jesus's entire ministry continues undiminished even as he walks toward his own death.

Jesus touches their eyes (hepsato ton ommaton auton). The word omma (eye) is distinct from the more common ophthalmos used elsewhere in the document. It is a rarer, more literary term. The touch is direct — Jesus makes physical contact with the site of their affliction. "Immediately" (eutheos) they received their sight. The healing is instantaneous and complete.

The final phrase — "and followed him" (kai ekolouthesain auto) — is weighty. The verb akoloutheo (to follow) is the document's standard term for discipleship. At 4:20, 22, the first disciples left their nets and "followed him." At 8:22, Jesus said "follow me" to the would-be disciple. At 9:9, Matthew rose and "followed him." At 16:24, "If anyone wishes to come after Me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross and follow Me." At 19:21, Jesus told the rich young man, "Come, follow Me" — and the young man could not. At 19:27, Peter said, "We have left everything and followed You." Now the two formerly blind men follow Jesus — and the direction of their following is toward Jerusalem, toward the passion. They are following a man walking to his death. Their following, unlike the rich young man's inability to follow, is immediate and unreserved. They have received their sight and they use it to follow the one who gave it.

div.title: The Chapter's Function in the Author's Larger Argument

list.item: It dismantles a transactional understanding of the kingdom's reward system. Peter's question in 19:27 — "what will there be for us?" — was legitimate, and Jesus answered it with genuine promises (19:28-29). But the parable of the vineyard laborers (20:1-16) prevents those promises from being understood as proportional compensation. The kingdom's economy is the landowner's generosity, not the laborer's merit. Those who came first and those who came last receive the same denarius. The complaint of the first-hired is exposed as an "evil eye" — an inability to celebrate another's blessing because one is fixated on comparative advantage. The parable does not cancel reward; it redefines the basis of reward as the giver's goodness rather than the receiver's achievement.

It provides the most detailed passion prediction in the document and uses it as the foundation for the teaching that follows. The third prediction (20:17-19) specifies what the first two left general: handing over to chief priests and scribes, condemnation to death, delivery to Gentiles, mocking, flogging, crucifixion, resurrection. Each detail brings the coming suffering into sharper focus. The author places this prediction between the vineyard parable and the request of Zebedee's sons so that the teaching on servant-leadership (20:25-28) rests on the concrete reality of what the Son of Man is about to undergo. The servant-leadership ethic is not an abstract ideal; it is grounded in the specific historical act of Jesus's suffering and death.

It exposes the persistence of status-seeking among the disciples despite repeated correction. The request of the mother of Zebedee's sons (20:20-21) and the indignation of the ten (20:24) reveal that the entire group of twelve still operates on the assumption that the kingdom is a hierarchy of honor to be climbed. This comes after the child-as-model teaching (18:1-5), the first-last reversal (19:30), and the vineyard parable (20:1-16). The disciples' failure to internalize what they have been taught is not incidental — it is part of the author's sustained portrait of a community that has been given extraordinary teaching and still struggles to comprehend it. The gap between what the disciples know and what they do is a recurring theme (cf. 16:22-23, 17:17, 19:13-14), and here it is at its starkest: Jesus describes his death and they ask for thrones.

It defines the fundamental ethic of the community as service, grounded in the Son of Man's own example. The servant-leadership teaching (20:25-28) is not a suggestion but a constitutive description of how the community is to function. The Gentile model of authority-as-domination is explicitly excluded: "It is not this way among you." The kingdom model is authority-as-service: whoever wants to be great must be a diakonos; whoever wants to be first must be a doulos. The Son of Man himself is the paradigm: he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. The ethic is christological — it flows from who Jesus is and what he does, not from an abstract principle of humility. Service is the shape of the kingdom because service is the shape of its king.

It presents the lytron (ransom) saying as the theological ground for the Son of Man's death. The statement that the Son of Man came "to give his life as a ransom for many" (20:28) is the most concentrated soteriological statement in the document. It connects Jesus's death to the redemption vocabulary of the LXX (lytroo, lytron), to the Servant of Isaiah 53 who bears the sin of many, and to the Passover/exodus tradition of God paying the price to liberate his people from bondage. The death is not merely exemplary (showing how to serve) but effective (accomplishing something for "the many"). The ransom-language indicates a release procured at a cost — and the cost is the Son of Man's life.

It demonstrates the Son of Man's servant mission in the healing of the two blind men. The chapter moves from teaching about service (vv. 25-28) to the enactment of service (vv. 29-34). The blind men are the kind of people the kingdom's inverted values prioritize — marginalized, silenced by the crowd, dependent on mercy. Jesus stops for them, touches them, heals them. His compassion (splagchnizomai) is the same visceral mercy that characterized the king in the parable of 18:27 and that defined Jesus's ministry from its beginning. The blind men's response — they follow him — completes the pattern: they received what the rich young man could not bring himself to receive (the call to follow), and they join Jesus on the road to Jerusalem. Their physical sight restored, they follow the one heading toward the cross.

It creates a sustained contrast between those who see and those who are blind. The disciples have physical sight but cannot see what Jesus has been telling them — they hear about his death and ask for thrones. The crowd has eyes but tries to silence the ones crying for mercy. The blind men cannot see but correctly identify Jesus as the Son of David and ask for the right thing. The "evil eye" of the grumbling laborer (20:15) is the eye that sees only comparative advantage and misses the owner's goodness. The opened eyes of the healed blind men see Jesus and follow him. Across the chapter, sight is not physical but spiritual, and the author uses the contrast to force the reader to ask: who actually sees? The answer, consistently, is not those who assume they deserve more but those who know they need mercy.

div.title: Matthew 21 — First-Century Reading
Context Within the Author's Argument
div.p: What came before (Matthew 20): The author continued the thread begun at 19:30 ("many who are first will be last, and the last first") with the parable of the workers in the vineyard (20:1-16), in which those hired at the eleventh hour received the same wage as those who labored all day. The parable ended with the identical statement in reverse order: "So the last will be first, and the first last" (20:16). The landowner's response to the grumbling workers was sharp: "Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" (20:15). The parable thus established that the kingdom operates on the principle of the owner's sovereign generosity, not the workers' calculation of merit — and that those who consider themselves first by virtue of longer service may find themselves resentful of the grace extended to latecomers. Jesus then delivered the third and most detailed passion prediction (20:17-19): "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day." This is the first time crucifixion is explicitly named, and the first time the role of the Gentiles is specified. The mother of James and John then asked Jesus to grant her sons seats at his right and left in his kingdom (20:20-21), exposing the disciples' persistent inability to understand the nature of Jesus's kingship. Jesus responded: "You do not know what you are asking" (20:22), and taught that greatness in his community is defined by servanthood: "Whoever would be great among you must be your servant (diakonos), and whoever would be first among you must be your slave (doulos), even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (20:26-28). The chapter closed at Jericho, where two blind men cried out, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!" (20:30-31). Despite the crowd's attempt to silence them, Jesus stopped, was "moved with compassion" (splagchnistheis, 20:34), and healed them. They followed him. The chapter thus moved from sovereign generosity (the vineyard parable) to the explicit prediction of death in Jerusalem, to the redefinition of greatness as servanthood, to the healing of the blind who recognized Jesus as Son of David — and the road now leads directly to Jerusalem.

What comes after (Matthew 22): The confrontation with the religious leadership that dominates chapter 21 intensifies in chapter 22. Jesus tells the parable of the wedding feast (22:1-14), in which a king sends invitations to a marriage feast for his son, but the invited guests refuse to come — some making light of it, others killing the messengers. The king destroys those murderers and burns their city (22:7), then sends servants into the streets to gather "both bad and good" (22:10). When the king finds a guest without a wedding garment, that man is cast into "the outer darkness" where there is "weeping and gnashing of teeth" (22:13), and Jesus concludes: "For many are called, but few are chosen" (22:14). The parable extends the vineyard tenants parable of 21:33-46 by moving from Israel's leaders who rejected and killed the prophets to the broader question of who will actually participate in the kingdom and on what terms. The Pharisees then attempt to trap Jesus with a question about paying taxes to Caesar (22:15-22); the Sadducees test him on the resurrection (22:23-33); a lawyer asks about the greatest commandment (22:34-40); and Jesus himself poses a question about David's Son and David's Lord (22:41-46) that silences them all: "No one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions" (22:46). Chapter 22 thus completes the pattern begun in chapter 21: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the one to whom the kingdom's authority belongs, confronts the religious leadership's failure, tells parables that announce the transfer of the kingdom from those who rejected the owner's messengers to those who will produce its fruit, and then answers and silences every challenge the leadership can mount.

How chapter 21 connects them: Chapter 20 ended on the road from Jericho to Jerusalem, with the third passion prediction fresh and the blind men's acclamation of Jesus as "Son of David" still in the air. Chapter 21 is the arrival. Everything that has been building since 16:21 — the passion predictions, the teaching about servanthood, the journey to Jerusalem — now reaches the city itself. Jesus enters Jerusalem in a manner that deliberately enacts the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9, presenting himself publicly as Israel's king. But the kingship he enacts is the paradoxical one the author has been constructing: he comes "humble" (praus), mounted on a donkey, not a warhorse. The "Son of David" acclamation that the blind men at Jericho spoke privately now erupts from the crowds in the streets of Jerusalem. Once inside the city, Jesus goes immediately to the temple and overturns the tables — an act of prophetic judgment that draws on Jeremiah 7 and Isaiah 56 and asserts his authority over the center of Israel's religious life. The rest of the chapter consists of a sustained confrontation between Jesus and the chief priests and elders, conducted through the question of authority (vv. 23-27) and two parables (the two sons, vv. 28-32; the tenants, vv. 33-46) that together constitute an indictment: Israel's leaders have failed to respond to God's messengers, failed to produce the fruit God requires, and will see the kingdom transferred from them to others. The movement from chapter 20's road to Jerusalem through chapter 21's arrival and confrontation to chapter 22's escalating tests is continuous — it is the single sustained narrative of Jesus's final days in Jerusalem, where the clash between his authority and the religious establishment's authority comes to its decisive point.

div.title: The Entry into Jerusalem: Zechariah's King Enacted (vv. 1-11)
div.p: "And when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them, 'Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her (onon dedemenon kai polon met' autes). Untie them and bring them to me. If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, "The Lord needs them," and he will send them at once.'"

The geography is precise. Bethphage is a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, the last settlement before Jerusalem on the road from Jericho. The Mount of Olives carries its own prophetic weight: Zechariah 14:4 declares that "on that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives that lies before Jerusalem on the east," followed by the LORD's coming with all his holy ones and the establishment of his universal kingship (Zechariah 14:9). The author places Jesus at precisely the location where Zechariah located the LORD's eschatological arrival.

The instruction to find a donkey and a colt is distinctive. The author specifies both animals — "a donkey tied, and a colt with her" — where the parallel accounts in Mark (11:2) and Luke (19:30) mention only the colt. This doubling corresponds to the author's reading of Zechariah 9:9, which he is about to cite.

"This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying, 'Say to the daughter of Zion, "Behold, your king is coming to you, humble (praus), and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden (epi onon kai epi polon huion hypozugiou)."'"

The citation combines Isaiah 62:11 ("Say to the daughter of Zion") with Zechariah 9:9. The Zechariah text in Hebrew uses parallelism — "humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey" — where the two lines describe the same animal in parallel. The author appears to read the text as describing two animals, and accordingly has Jesus ride with both the donkey and the colt present. Whether the author intends a literal two-animal reading or is simply preserving the wording of the prophecy with both terms present, the theological point is the same: Jesus is enacting the arrival of Zechariah's king.

The critical word in the citation is praus — "humble" or "gentle." This is the same word Jesus used to describe himself at 11:29: "I am gentle (praus) and lowly (tapeinos) in heart." It is the same word from the third beatitude: "Blessed are the meek (praeis), for they shall inherit the earth" (5:5). The king who enters Jerusalem is defined by the same quality that defines his followers. He does not come on a warhorse, as a conquering general would, but on a donkey — the animal of peace, of the working peasant, of humble daily labor. The entry is a deliberate contrast to every expectation of military triumph. Zechariah 9:9 itself makes this explicit: the verse continues (in the Hebrew text, though the author does not cite this portion) with "I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations." The king who comes on a donkey is the king who abolishes the instruments of war.
"The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks (epetheken epano auton ta himatia), and he sat on them."

The placing of cloaks on the animals echoes 2 Kings 9:13, where Jehu's officers spread their garments under him on the steps when he was proclaimed king. The garments function as an improvised royal covering — the disciples are preparing a throne, however humble, for the one they recognize as king.
"Most of the crowd (ho de pleistos ochlos) spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road."

The spreading of garments on the road is again royal language, as in the Jehu episode. The cutting of branches recalls the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot), when palm and other branches were waved in celebration (Leviticus 23:40). In 1 Maccabees 13:51, when Simon Maccabeus entered the citadel of Jerusalem after expelling the Gentile garrison, the people entered "with praise and palm branches, and with harps and cymbals and stringed instruments, and with hymns and songs." The crowd is greeting Jesus with the gestures reserved for a king entering his city.

"And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, 'Hosanna to the Son of David (hosanna to huio Dauid)! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord (eulogemenos ho erchomenos en onomati kyriou)! Hosanna in the highest (hosanna en tois hypsistois)!'"

"Hosanna" (hosanna) is a transliteration of the Hebrew hoshi'a na, meaning "Save, please!" or "Save now!" It comes from Psalm 118:25: "Save us, we pray, O LORD! O LORD, we pray, give us success!" Psalm 118 is a processional psalm used at major festivals, particularly Tabernacles and Passover. The next verse of the psalm — "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD" (Psalm 118:26) — is what the crowd cites. In its original setting, this blessing was spoken by the priests to the worshippers entering the temple. Here it is directed at Jesus as a messianic acclamation. The phrase "he who comes" (ho erchomenos) carries eschatological weight: at 11:3, John the Baptist from prison asked, "Are you the one who is to come (ho erchomenos), or shall we look for another?" The crowd answers the question John asked.

The title "Son of David" (huios Dauid) has appeared at critical moments: the genealogy's opening (1:1), the blind men's cry (9:27, 20:30-31), the Canaanite woman's appeal (15:22), and the crowd's astonishment at 12:23 ("Can this be the Son of David?"). Now it is publicly proclaimed as Jesus enters the capital. The Davidic claim is being made in the city of David, within sight of David's throne.

"And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred (eseisthe pasa he polis), saying, 'Who is this (tis estin houtos)?' And the crowds said, 'This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee (houtos estin ho prophetes Iesous ho apo Nazareth tes Galilaias).'"

The verb seio (to shake, to quake) is striking. The author uses this word for earthquakes — it will appear at 27:51 when the earth shakes at Jesus's death and at 28:2 when the earth shakes at his resurrection. The city "was shaken" — the arrival of the king is seismic. The same word appeared at 2:3, when "all Jerusalem was troubled" (etarachthe) at the report of the magi; now at the other end of the narrative, the city shakes again at Jesus's entry. The two responses form a frame: Jerusalem was disturbed by news of the king's birth, and Jerusalem quakes at the king's arrival. Both times, the city asks who this is, and both times, the identification carries threat.

The crowd identifies Jesus as "the prophet ... from Nazareth of Galilee." The identification as "the prophet" (ho prophetes) with the definite article may allude to the prophet-like-Moses of Deuteronomy 18:15, the same text echoed at the transfiguration ("listen to him," 17:5). But the qualifier "from Nazareth of Galilee" also underscores the irony: Galilee is not where the authorities expect the Messiah to originate (cf. John 7:41, 52), and Nazareth is the obscure village from which Nathanael asked, "Can anything good come?" (John 1:46). The one who shakes Jerusalem comes from the margins.

div.title: The Temple Cleansed: Prophetic Judgment on Israel's Worship (vv. 12-17)
div.p: "And Jesus entered the temple (to hieron) and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers (ton kollybiston) and the seats of those who sold pigeons (ton polounton tas peristeras)."

The term hieron refers to the entire temple complex, not just the inner sanctuary (naos). The commercial activity Jesus disrupts was located in the Court of the Gentiles — the outermost court of the temple, the only area where non-Jews could come to pray. Money-changers (kollybistai) were necessary because the temple tax had to be paid in Tyrian shekels (the only currency accepted for temple payments, due to its silver purity), so pilgrims carrying Roman or other coinage needed to exchange it. The pigeon sellers provided the sacrificial animals required by Torah for the purification offerings of the poor (Leviticus 5:7, 12:8). These commercial activities were not inherently illegitimate — they served the temple's ritual functions. Jesus's action is not directed against commerce as such but against what the commerce has become, as the next verse explains.
"He said to them, 'It is written, "My house shall be called a house of prayer (oikos proseuchis klethesetai)," but you make it a den of robbers (spelaion leston).'"

The statement combines two prophetic texts. The first is Isaiah 56:7: "My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples" (LXX: ho gar oikos mou oikos proseuches klethesetai pasin tois ethnesin). The full text of Isaiah 56:7 includes "for all peoples" (pasin tois ethnesin) — the house of prayer is specifically for the nations, for the Gentiles. This is significant because the commercial activity occupied the Court of the Gentiles — the very space where non-Jews were supposed to be able to approach God in prayer. The commerce had colonized the space designated for Gentile worship.

The second text is Jeremiah 7:11: "Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers (spelaion leston) in your eyes?" Jeremiah 7 is the prophet's temple sermon, delivered at the gate of the temple, warning Israel not to trust in the words "the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD" (Jeremiah 7:4) while practicing injustice, oppression, and idolatry. Jeremiah's point was that the temple had become a refuge for those who practiced wickedness — a "den" (spelaion, cave) to which robbers retreat after committing their crimes, feeling safe because they are in sacred space. The temple does not sanctify those who misuse it; it indicts them. Jesus is placing himself in the role of Jeremiah, pronouncing the same judgment: the temple has become a place where those who exploit and oppress take refuge under the cover of religious legitimacy.

The word lestai (robbers, bandits) is stronger than "thieves" (kleptai). A lestes is a violent criminal, a bandit — the word used for those crucified alongside Jesus (27:38, 44) and for Barabbas in some traditions. The accusation is not of petty theft but of systemic exploitation carried out under the protection of sacred space.
"And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them (kai proselthon auto typhloi kai choloi en to hiero, kai etherapeusen autous)."

This detail, unique to the author's account, is theologically charged. In 2 Samuel 5:8, after David captured Jerusalem, a saying arose: "The blind and the lame shall not come into the house." This was understood to exclude the physically disabled from the temple. Jesus, having just cleared the temple of its commercial operations, immediately fills the space with the very people who were excluded. The Son of David's temple is not a marketplace for the privileged but a place of healing for the marginalized. The action demonstrates in concrete terms what the temple was meant to be: a house of prayer where God's restorative power is available to all, including those whom the existing order excluded.

"But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did (tas thaumasias ha epoiesen), and the children crying out in the temple, 'Hosanna to the Son of David!' they were indignant (eganaktesan)."

The chief priests and scribes respond to two things: the healings and the children's acclamation. The children in the temple are shouting the same "Hosanna to the Son of David" that the crowds shouted at the entry. The leadership is "indignant" (aganakteo — the same word used at 20:24 when the ten disciples were indignant at James and John's request for positions of honor). Their indignation is provoked by the messianic title being used in the temple — the claim that this Galilean is the Son of David, spoken in the very precinct where David's heir exercises authority. The Davidic claim, made in the temple, is a direct challenge to the authority of the chief priests who administer it.

"And they said to him, 'Do you hear what these are saying?' And Jesus said to them, 'Yes; have you never read, "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise (ek stomatos nepion kai thelazonton katertiso ainon)"?'"

Jesus responds with Psalm 8:2 (LXX 8:3): "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise." In the original psalm, this is addressed to God — it is God who has ordained praise from the youngest and weakest to silence the enemy and the avenger. Jesus applies this text to himself: the praise directed at him by children is the praise that God himself has prepared. The implication is that to silence the children's Hosannas would be to oppose what God has ordained. The chief priests, who should recognize the fulfillment of scripture when it occurs in their own temple, are instead offended by it. The contrast is sharp: children and the blind and lame recognize who Jesus is; the religious experts do not.
"And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany (Bethanian) and lodged there."

Jesus withdraws to Bethany, about two miles east of Jerusalem on the far side of the Mount of Olives. This pattern of entering Jerusalem by day and withdrawing at night continues through the passion week. Bethany is the home of Lazarus, Martha, and Mary (John 11:1; cf. Matthew 26:6, "the house of Simon the leper" in Bethany). The withdrawal may reflect practical safety — Jerusalem is hostile territory — but it also creates a daily rhythm of approach and departure that frames the confrontations of the following days.

div.title: The Fig Tree Cursed: Enacted Judgment on Fruitlessness (vv. 18-22)
div.p: "In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves (ei me phylla monon). And he said to it, 'May no fruit ever come from you again (ou meketi ek sou karpos genetai eis ton aiona)!' And the fig tree withered at once (exeranthe parachrema he syke)."

This action must be read as a prophetic sign-act, not a personal expression of frustration. The prophets of Israel frequently performed symbolic actions that enacted the reality they proclaimed: Isaiah walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt and Cush (Isaiah 20:2-4); Jeremiah smashed a potter's flask at the Valley of Hinnom (Jeremiah 19:1-13); Ezekiel lay on his side for 390 days (Ezekiel 4:4-6). The cursing of the fig tree belongs to this tradition of enacted prophecy.

The fig tree in Israel's prophetic literature consistently represents Israel itself or its leadership. Jeremiah 8:13: "When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered." Hosea 9:10: "Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel. Like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers." Micah 7:1: "Woe is me! For I have become as when the summer fruit has been gathered, as when the grapes have been gleaned: there is no cluster to eat, no first-ripe fig that my soul desires." Joel 1:7: "It has laid waste my vine and splintered my fig tree." In each case, the absence of fruit on the fig tree signifies Israel's failure to produce the response God sought.

The phrase "nothing on it but only leaves" is the critical detail. The tree has the appearance of fruitfulness — leaves suggest life and health — but produces no actual fruit. This is precisely the accusation the author has been building through the preceding episodes. The temple has all the external apparatus of worship — the commerce, the ritual, the institutional structure — but has become a "den of robbers" rather than a "house of prayer." The religious leadership has the credentials and authority but does not recognize the one whom God has sent. The fig tree with leaves but no fruit is an enacted parable of the temple establishment: impressive in appearance, barren in substance.

The immediate withering (exeranthe parachrema — "dried up at once") intensifies the sign. In the parallel account in Mark (11:12-14, 20-21), the disciples do not notice the withering until the next morning. The author compresses the timeline so that the consequence is instantaneous, emphasizing the immediacy of the judgment.

"When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, 'How did the fig tree wither at once (pos parachrema exeranthe he syke)?' And Jesus answered them, 'Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt (ean echete pistin kai me diakrithete), you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, "Be taken up and thrown into the sea," it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith (ean pisteuete).'"

The disciples ask about mechanism — how did the tree wither so quickly? Jesus redirects to the principle: faith that does not doubt (me diakrithete — the verb diakrino means to waver, to be divided in one's mind) can accomplish even greater things. The reference to "this mountain" (to orei touto) is not generic. Jesus is standing between the Mount of Olives and Jerusalem, within sight of the temple mount. The mountain cast into the sea may echo the prophetic tradition of Zechariah 14:10, where the land around Jerusalem is leveled, and it may anticipate Jesus's own prophecy of the temple's destruction (24:1-2). In context, the saying addresses the disciples' capacity to participate in God's acts of judgment and restoration through faith and prayer.

The connection to the immediately preceding sign-act is important. The fig tree's judgment was an act of divine power channeled through Jesus's word. Jesus tells the disciples that they, through faith, have access to the same power. The community formed around Jesus is not merely an audience to his prophetic acts but a participant in them. The condition, however, is faith without internal division — a condition that recalls the "little faith" (oligopistia) the author has repeatedly diagnosed in the disciples (6:30, 8:26, 14:31, 16:8, 17:20).

div.title: The Question of Authority: John and Jesus (vv. 23-27)
div.p: "And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, 'By what authority are you doing these things (en poia exousia tauta poieis), and who gave you this authority (kai tis soi edoken ten exousian tauten)?'"

The question comes from the two groups who hold official power in Jerusalem: the chief priests (archiereis), who control the temple, and the elders of the people (presbyteroi tou laou), who form the lay aristocracy of the Sanhedrin. Together they represent the institutional authority of Israel. Their question is pointed: "By what authority?" (en poia exousia — literally, "in what kind of authority"). The word exousia (authority, right, power) has been a central term in the document. At 7:29, the crowds recognized that Jesus taught "as one having authority" (hos exousian echon) in contrast to their scribes. At 9:6, Jesus claimed "authority on earth to forgive sins." At 10:1, he gave the twelve "authority over unclean spirits." At 28:18, the risen Jesus will declare, "All authority (pasa exousia) in heaven and on earth has been given to me." The chief priests' question is whether Jesus possesses the kind of authority that would justify his actions in the temple — the overturning of tables, the healings, the teaching. The implicit accusation is that he does not; he has no institutional sanction, no appointment, no official standing.

"These things" (tauta) refers not merely to his current teaching but to the entirety of what he has done since entering Jerusalem: the public entry as messianic king, the disruption of the temple commerce, the healings, the acceptance of the Hosanna acclamations. All of these are acts that claim an authority the leadership has not conferred.

"Jesus answered them, 'I also will ask you one question (eroteso hymas kago logon hena), and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John, from where did it come (to baptisma to Ioannou pothen en)? From heaven or from man (ex ouranou e ex anthropon)?'"

Jesus does not refuse to answer; he poses a counter-question that exposes the structure of the problem. The question about John's baptism is not a deflection but a diagnostic: if the chief priests and elders can correctly identify the source of John's authority, they will have the answer to their own question about Jesus's authority. John announced Jesus (3:11-12); John baptized Jesus (3:13-17); Jesus himself identified John as the Elijah who was to come (11:14, 17:12-13). To acknowledge that John's baptism was "from heaven" (ex ouranou) — that is, authorized by God — is to acknowledge the divine authority behind the one John pointed to. The question about John's authority and the question about Jesus's authority are the same question.

"And they discussed it among themselves, saying, 'If we say, "From heaven," he will say to us, "Why then did you not believe him?" But if we say, "From man," we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet.'"

The leaders' deliberation reveals that their question was not sincere inquiry but political calculation. They are not seeking truth; they are managing risk. If they affirm John's divine authorization, they indict themselves for not responding to his message — which would mean accepting Jesus. If they deny John's divine authorization, they face the crowd, who regard John as a prophet. Their inability to answer is not ignorance but willful evasion. They know the implications of both answers and refuse to accept either.
"So they answered Jesus, 'We do not know (ouk oidamen).' And he said to them, 'Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things (oude ego lego hymin en poia exousia tauta poio).'"

The leaders' "we do not know" is not an honest confession of uncertainty but a strategic refusal to commit. Jesus's response matches their evasion: if they will not engage honestly with the evidence already before them (John's ministry, which pointed to Jesus), then further declaration from Jesus would serve no purpose. The exchange demonstrates a principle the author has established from the parables discourse onward (13:10-17): understanding is given to those who respond to what they have already received, and it is withheld from those who refuse to engage. The chief priests' refusal to answer about John disqualifies them from receiving a direct answer about Jesus.

div.title: The Parable of the Two Sons: Doing versus Saying (vv. 28-32)
div.p: "'What do you think (ti de hymin dokei)? A man had two sons (anthropos eichen tekna duo). And he went to the first and said, "Son, go and work in the vineyard today (teknon, hypage semeron ergazou en to ampeloni)." And he answered, "I will not (ou thelo)," but afterward he changed his mind and went (hysteron metameletheis apelthen). And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, "I go, sir (ego, kyrie)," but did not go.'"

The parable is addressed directly to the chief priests and elders (v. 23) — the same group that asked about authority. The vineyard (ampelon) is an immediately recognizable image for Israel in the prophetic tradition. Isaiah 5:1-7 is the controlling text: "The vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant planting." When the author uses "vineyard" in a parable directed at Israel's leadership, the first-century hearer knows the referent.

The first son initially refuses — "I will not" (ou thelo) — but then metameletheis (having changed his mind, having felt regret) goes to work. The verb metamelomai is distinct from metanoeo (to repent). Metamelomai denotes a change of feeling or purpose, a regret about one's previous decision, leading to a reversal of action. It does not carry the same theological weight as metanoeo but describes the practical reality: the son reversed course and did what the father asked.

The second son says "I go, sir" (ego, kyrie) — the address is respectful, the promise is immediate — but he does not go. His response has every mark of compliance: verbal agreement, honorific address, no objection. But it produces no action. The parable isolates the difference between speech and conduct, between profession and performance.

"'Which of the two did the will of his father (tis ek ton duo epoiesen to thelema tou patros)?' They said, 'The first.' Jesus said to them, 'Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you (hoi telonai kai hai pornai proagousin hymas eis ten basileian tou theou).'"

The chief priests and elders are forced to answer their own indictment. The one who "did the will of the father" (epoiesen to thelema tou patros) is not the one who said the right words but the one who ultimately acted. The phrase "the will of the father" echoes 7:21: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." The parallel is exact: saying "Lord, Lord" without doing the Father's will is the second son. The verbal profession without corresponding action is precisely what Jesus condemned at the climax of the Sermon on the Mount.

The identification of the two sons is then made explicit. The tax collectors and prostitutes are the first son: they initially lived in open defiance of God's will, but when John came preaching repentance, they believed and changed course. The chief priests and elders are the second son: they profess obedience, hold the positions of religious authority, say the right words — but they did not respond to John's message, and they are not responding to Jesus.

"'For John came to you in the way of righteousness (en hodo dikaiosynes), and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it (kai hymeis idontes), you did not afterward change your minds and believe him (oude metemelethesan hysteron tou pisteusai auto).'"

The phrase "the way of righteousness" (en hodo dikaiosynes) describes John's ministry. In LXX usage, "the way of righteousness" is a path of conduct consistent with God's requirements (Proverbs 8:20, 12:28, 16:31). John came embodying and proclaiming righteous conduct — specifically, repentance and the fruits worthy of repentance (3:8). The leadership did not believe him. Tax collectors and prostitutes — the very categories that represent the most despised members of society, those furthest from institutional religion — believed and responded. And even after seeing these transformations, the leadership still did not change their minds (metemelethesan, the same verb used for the first son's change of direction). The indictment is layered: they rejected John, they rejected the evidence of transformed lives, and they are now rejecting Jesus. Each layer deepens their culpability. Seeing and not responding is worse than not seeing at all — a principle the author established in 11:20-24, where the cities that saw Jesus's mighty works and did not repent would face harsher judgment than Sodom.

div.title: The Parable of the Tenants: The Vineyard Transferred (vv. 33-46)
div.p: "'Hear another parable (allen parabolen akousate). There was a master of a house (anthropos oikodespotes) who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower, and leased it to tenants (georgois), and went into another country.'"

The language is drawn directly and unmistakably from Isaiah 5:1-2 (LXX): "My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a winepress in it." Every detail — the planting, the fence, the winepress, the tower — recapitulates Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard. Any first-century Jewish listener steeped in the prophetic writings would recognize the allusion immediately. In Isaiah 5:7, the identification is explicit: "For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel." The author is telling a story about Israel, using Israel's own self-description.

The innovation in Jesus's version is the tenants (georgoi — farmers, vine-dressers). In Isaiah 5, the vineyard itself was the problem — "he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry" (Isaiah 5:7). In Jesus's parable, the vineyard is not defective; the tenants are. The vineyard (Israel, or more precisely, the kingdom of God's purposes for Israel) is good. The problem lies with those entrusted to manage it — the leadership.

"'When the season for fruit drew near (hote de engisen ho kairos ton karpon), he sent his servants (tous doulous autou) to the tenants to get his fruit (labein tous karpous autou). And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first (pleionis ton proton). And they did the same to them.'"

The owner's expectation is fruit (karpos). The word karpos has been a governing term since 3:8, where John the Baptist demanded "fruit worthy of repentance" (karpon axion tes metanoias). At 7:16-20, Jesus established the principle: "You will recognize them by their fruits" (apo ton karpon auton epignosesthe autous), and "every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire." At 12:33, "the tree is known by its fruit." The fig tree that was just cursed (vv. 18-19) bore no fruit. Throughout the document, fruit is the visible evidence of genuine response to God. The owner's sending of servants to collect fruit is God's sending of prophets to Israel to receive the response due to him.

The servants (douloi) represent the prophets. The treatment they receive — beaten, killed, stoned — recapitulates Israel's history of rejecting and killing its prophets. The tradition of Israel's violence against the prophets was well established: 2 Chronicles 24:20-21 records the stoning of Zechariah son of Jehoiada in the court of the temple; 1 Kings 19:10 has Elijah lamenting, "The people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword"; Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned (Jeremiah 20:2, 37:15); tradition held that Isaiah was sawn in two. Jesus himself will invoke this pattern explicitly at 23:29-37: "You build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous... so you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets."

The detail that the owner sends "more than the first" (pleionis ton proton) shows patience and escalation — God did not give up after the first rejection but sent more messengers. The tenants' response remained the same.

"'Finally he sent his son to them (hysteron de apesteilen pros autous ton huion autou), saying, "They will respect my son (entrapesontai ton huion mou)." But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, "This is the heir (houtos estin ho kleronomos). Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance (kai schomen ten kleronomian autou)." And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him (kai labontes auton exebalon exo tou ampelonos kai apekteinan).'"

The escalation from servants to son is the theological climax. The owner's decision to send his son represents a qualitative shift: the son is not merely another messenger but the heir (kleronomos), the one who has a relationship to the vineyard that no servant has. The father's expectation — "they will respect my son" (entrapesontai, from entrepo, to turn toward, to regard with respect, to feel shame before) — expresses the reasonable hope that the heir's status will elicit a different response than the servants received.
