The chief priests who arranged the payment of blood money and refused to accept responsibility when Judas returned it now demonstrate scrupulous concern about the ritual propriety of placing the coins back in the treasury. They are careful about the technicality (Deuteronomy 23:18 prohibits bringing the "wages of a dog" — tainted money — into the house of the LORD) while having already violated the substance. They strain out the gnat and swallow the camel (23:24). The word korbanan (treasury, from the Hebrew qorban, an offering to God, cf. Mark 7:11) is used only here in the document, identifying the specific temple fund for sacred purposes.

Their solution — purchasing a potter's field for burying strangers — uses the blood money for a purpose connected to death. The field becomes a place for the dead, purchased with death's price. The author notes: "Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood (agros haimatos) to this day" (v. 8). The phrase "to this day" (heos tes semeron) is an authorial aside directed at the reader, indicating that the name persisted into the time of writing — a well-known landmark in Jerusalem that first-century readers could verify.

"Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah (tote epleerothe to rethen dia Ieremiou tou prophetou), saying, 'And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me.'"

The author attributes the quotation to Jeremiah, though the language primarily reflects Zechariah 11:12-13: "So they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver. Then the LORD said to me, 'Throw it to the potter' — the lordly price at which I was priced by them. So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the LORD, to the potter." In Zechariah's enacted parable, the prophet represents a shepherd of Israel who is rejected by the flock; the "thirty pieces of silver" is the insultingly low wage assessed by the people for his service (thirty shekels was the price of a slave in Exodus 21:32). The rejected shepherd throws the silver into the temple, to the potter. The pattern is replicated: Jesus, the shepherd of Israel (cf. 2:6, 9:36, 25:32, 26:31), is valued at the price of a slave, and the money ends up in the temple and is used to purchase a potter's field.

The attribution to "Jeremiah" rather than Zechariah has been noted since antiquity. Several possibilities present themselves from a first-century perspective. Jeremiah 19:1-13 describes Jeremiah purchasing a potter's earthen flask and then smashing it in the valley of the son of Hinnom (Topheth), declaring that the place would be renamed "the Valley of Slaughter" because of the blood shed there, and that Jerusalem would become "like Topheth" — a place of death and burial. Jeremiah 32:6-15 records Jeremiah's purchase of a field as a prophetic sign. The author may be combining Zechariah's specific language about the thirty pieces of silver with Jeremiah's broader thematic context of the purchase of a field, the potter, and the renaming of a place of death. In some first-century textual traditions, the Book of the Twelve (minor prophets) was sometimes subsumed under the heading of a major prophet who preceded them. The author's citation practice treats the combined allusion as primarily Jeremianic in its thematic scope, even though the verbal details come from Zechariah.

div.title: Jesus Before Pilate: The Question of Kingship (vv. 11-14)
div.p: "Now Jesus stood before the governor (ho de Iesous estathe emprosthen tou hegemonos), and the governor asked him, 'Are you the King of the Jews (sy ei ho basileus ton Ioudaion)?' Jesus said, 'You have said so (sy legeis).'"

The scene shifts to the Roman judicial proceeding. The charge before Pilate is political: "King of the Jews" (basileus ton Ioudaion). The Sanhedrin condemned Jesus on the religious charge of blasphemy (26:65); before Pilate, the charge is framed as a claim to royal authority — the only kind of charge that would matter to a Roman governor. A messianic claimant asserting kingship over Judea would constitute sedition against Rome.

Jesus's response "You have said so" (sy legeis) is the same form used at 26:25 (to Judas: "You have said so") and 26:64 (to the high priest: "You have said so"). The phrase is neither a simple affirmation nor a denial. It acknowledges the statement while distancing Jesus from the meaning Pilate attaches to it. Jesus is indeed king, but the nature of his kingship is not what the term "King of the Jews" means in Pilate's Roman framework.

"But when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer (ouk apekrinato... ouden). Then Pilate said to him, 'Do you not hear how many things they testify against you (posa sou katamartyrosin)?' But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge (ouk apekrithe auto pros oude hen rhema), so that the governor was greatly amazed (hoste thaumazein ton hegemona lian)."

Jesus's silence before accusation invokes Isaiah 53:7: "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth." The Isaianic servant is the one who suffers in silence, bearing the sins of others. The word rhema (word, utterance) emphasizes the completeness of the silence: not even a single word in response. The governor's amazement (thaumazo) indicates that silence in the face of capital charges was abnormal. A defendant who refused to defend himself defied the logic of Roman judicial procedure, in which self-defense was a right and an expectation. Pilate interprets Jesus's silence not as guilt but as something extraordinary.

div.title: The Release of Barabbas and the Condemnation of Jesus (vv. 15-26)
div.p: "Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted (hena desmion hon ethelon). And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas (desmion episemon legomenon Barabban)."

The custom of releasing a prisoner at the festival is attested by the author as an established practice (kata heorten — "at the feast"). The name Barabbas (Bar-Abba) means "son of the father" in Aramaic. The irony in the author's narrative is structural: the crowd will choose the "son of the father" (Barabbas) and reject the Son of the Father (Jesus, identified as God's Son at 3:17, 17:5). Some early manuscripts (attested by Origen) give Barabbas the name "Jesus Barabbas," which would sharpen the irony further: the crowd chooses between two men named Jesus, one the "son of the father" by name only, the other the Son of the Father by nature.

"So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, 'Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ (Iesoun ton legomenon Christon)?' For he knew that it was out of envy (dia phthonon) that they had delivered him up."

Pilate perceives the motive: "envy" (phthonos). The word denotes resentment of another's position, authority, or success. The chief priests and elders delivered Jesus to Pilate not because of a genuine legal violation but because of their jealousy of his influence. Pilate's insight functions as another testimony to Jesus's innocence from a hostile or indifferent source — Judas declared the blood "innocent" (v. 4), Pilate recognizes the motive as envy rather than justice.

"Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat (kathemenou autou epi tou bematos), his wife sent word to him, 'Have nothing to do with that righteous man (to dikaio ekeino), for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream (kat' onar).'"

Pilate's wife provides yet another testimony to Jesus's innocence, calling him "that righteous man" (ho dikaios ekeinos). Her warning comes through a dream (kat' onar) — the same mechanism by which God communicated to Joseph at the beginning of the document (1:20, 2:12, 13, 19, 22). In the author's narrative framework, dreams function as divine communication. A Gentile woman receives divine guidance about the identity of the righteous one, while the religious leadership of Israel has condemned him. The pattern echoes the magi in chapter 2: Gentiles receive divine direction, while Herod (the ruler) plots destruction.
"Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd (epeisan tous ochlous) to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus (hina aiteosontai ton Barabban ton de Iesoun apoleseosin)."

The verb peitho (to persuade, to convince) indicates active effort by the leadership to sway the crowd. The crowd does not spontaneously choose Barabbas; the chief priests and elders work to produce this outcome. The word apollymi (to destroy, to kill, to lose) is the same word used for Herod's attempt to destroy the child Jesus in 2:13 — the author uses the same verb for the threat at the beginning and at the end of the narrative.

"The governor again said to them, 'Which of the two do you want me to release for you?' And they said, 'Barabbas (ton Barabban).' Pilate said to them, 'Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ (ti oun poieso Iesoun ton legomenon Christon)?' They all said, 'Let him be crucified (staurotheto)!' And he said, 'Why? What evil has he done (ti gar kakon epoiesen)?' But they shouted all the more, 'Let him be crucified!'"

Pilate's question "What evil has he done?" constitutes yet another declaration of innocence — this time from the judge himself. The governor who is supposed to condemn cannot identify the crime. The escalation from "let him be crucified" to the repeated shout "let him be crucified" portrays a crowd driven by the momentum of mob persuasion, not reasoned judgment. The verb stauroo (to crucify) appears here for the first time as a crowd demand, though Jesus predicted it at 20:19 and 26:2.

"So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing (ouden ophelei), but rather that a riot was beginning (alla mallon thorybos ginetai), he took water and washed his hands before the crowd (apenipsato tas cheiras apenanti tou ochlou), saying, 'I am innocent of this man's blood (athoos eimi apo tou haimatos toutou); see to it yourselves (hymeis opsesthe).'"

Pilate's hand-washing invokes Deuteronomy 21:6-7, where the elders of a city nearest to an unsolved murder wash their hands over a heifer and declare: "Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed." The ritual is Israelite in origin, and the author places it in the hands of a Roman governor. Pilate's declaration "I am innocent of this blood" (athoos eimi) uses the same word Judas used of Jesus — athoos (innocent, guiltless). Pilate claims innocence of Jesus's blood while having the authority and obligation to prevent an unjust execution. His words "see to it yourselves" (hymeis opsesthe) echo precisely what the chief priests said to Judas: "see to it yourself" (sy opse, v. 4). Both the religious leaders and the political ruler attempt to deflect responsibility, using the same phrase.
"And all the people answered, 'His blood be on us and on our children (to haima autou eph' hemas kai epi ta tekna hemon)!'"

The crowd's declaration assumes the legal language of blood guilt. In 2 Samuel 1:16, David says to the Amalekite who claimed to have killed Saul: "Your blood be on your head." In Joshua 2:19, Rahab is told that if anyone in her house goes into the street, "his blood shall be on his own head." The phrase indicates the acceptance of legal responsibility for the consequences of bloodshed. The crowd invokes this liability upon themselves "and upon our children" (epi ta tekna hemon), extending the responsibility across a generation. In the author's narrative, this connects directly to Jesus's warnings in chapter 23: "Upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth... Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation" (23:35-36). The crowd's self-imprecation and Jesus's prediction converge: the blood guilt they accept and the judgment Jesus announced upon "this generation" point to the same historical consequences. For the first-century reader who knew the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, the crowd's words carry the weight of fulfilled warning.

The author is not attributing guilt to an ethnic group in perpetuity but recording a specific crowd's specific declaration, which the author connects to a specific historical consequence that falls "upon this generation" — a temporally bounded judgment, not an eternal curse. The text's own framework, established by Jesus's repeated use of "this generation" (11:16, 12:39-45, 16:4, 17:17, 23:36, 24:34), confines the scope to the contemporaries.
"Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus (ton de Iesoun phragellosas), delivered him to be crucified (paredoken hina stauerothe)."

The scourging (phragellosas, from the Latin flagellum) was a Roman preliminary to crucifixion, involving a leather whip embedded with bone or metal fragments. Josephus records instances where scourging alone caused death (War 2.306-308). The verb paradidomi (to deliver over) appears again — Jesus is "delivered" yet another time in the chain that began with Judas and continued through the chief priests to Pilate. Each link in the chain fulfills Jesus's prediction at 20:18-19.

div.title: The Soldiers' Mockery of the King (vv. 27-31)
div.p: "Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor's headquarters (eis to praitorion), and they gathered the whole battalion (holen ten speiran) before him."

The praetorium (praitorion, from Latin praetorium) was the governor's residence and administrative center in Jerusalem, likely either the Antonia Fortress adjoining the temple or Herod's palace on the western hill. A "cohort" (speira) at full strength numbered 480-600 soldiers, though the word can denote a smaller detachment. The gathering of the whole unit indicates that the mockery is a collective act, not the impulse of a few individuals.

"And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him (chlamyda kokkinon), and twisting together a crown of thorns (stephanon ex akanthon), they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand (kalamon en te dexia autou). And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, 'Hail, King of the Jews! (chaire, basileu ton Ioudaion)'"

The mockery is structured as a parody of royal investiture. Each element corresponds to a genuine feature of kingship: the scarlet robe (chlamys kokkine) substitutes for the purple of royalty (Roman soldiers' cloaks were scarlet; the resemblance to purple made it useful for the parody); the crown of thorns replaces the laurel wreath or diadem; the reed (kalamos) replaces the royal scepter; the kneeling (gonypeteo) parodies the act of homage; and the greeting "Hail, King of the Jews" (chaire, basileu ton Ioudaion) parodies the acclamation "Ave, Caesar" (chaire, Kaisar). Every element of genuine kingship is inverted: the robe is a soldier's castoff, the crown is made of thorns that wound, the scepter is a fragile reed, and the homage is performed in mockery.

The author's sustained irony operates at every level: the soldiers mock what they do not know to be true. The reader, who has followed the narrative from the angelic announcement of 1:21 ("he will save his people from their sins") through the magi's question "Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?" (2:2), through the entry into Jerusalem when the crowds hailed him as "Son of David" (21:9), and through Jesus's own claim before the Sanhedrin to be "the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power" (26:64), understands that the soldiers are unwittingly enacting the truth. Jesus is the King of the Jews. The crown, the robe, the scepter, and the acclamation are all real — but in a register the soldiers cannot perceive.

"And they spit on him (eneptyon eis auton) and took the reed and struck him on the head (etypton eis ten kephalen autou). And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him (apegagon auton eis to staurosai)."

The spitting recalls Isaiah 50:6: "I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting." This is the third of the Isaianic servant songs, where the servant endures humiliation without resistance, trusting in the LORD's vindication. The striking with the reed — the mock scepter used as a weapon — encapsulates the entire scene: the symbol of authority is turned into an instrument of violence against the one who holds the authority.

div.title: The Crucifixion (vv. 32-44)
div.p: "As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name (Simona Kyrenaion). They compelled this man to carry his cross (egareusan hina are ton stauron autou)."

The verb agareuo (to compel, to requisition, to conscript) is a loan word from Persian, referring to the authority of royal couriers to commandeer labor, animals, or goods. It appeared at 5:41: "And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles." The same word describes Roman compulsion of a civilian — Simon of Cyrene is conscripted to carry the horizontal beam (patibulum) of the cross. Cyrene was a city in North Africa (modern Libya) with a significant Jewish population (cf. Acts 2:10, 6:9, 11:20). Simon is identified by name and origin, suggesting he may have been known to the early community.

"And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull, Kraniou Topos), they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall (oinon meta choles memigmenon), and when he tasted it, he would not drink it (ouk ethelesen piein)."

The location name "Place of a Skull" (Kraniou Topos, translating the Aramaic Golgotha/Gulgolta) likely refers to the appearance of the rock formation, a bare promontory outside the city walls. The wine mixed with gall (chole) draws on Psalm 69:21 (LXX 68:22): "They gave me poison (chole) for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink." The Psalm 69 connection is explicit through the word chole (gall, bile, poison). In the Psalm, the sufferer is a righteous one surrounded by enemies who heap abuse upon him. Jesus tastes the drink but refuses it — he will undergo the suffering without sedation or dulling of consciousness.
"And when they had crucified him (staurosantes de auton), they divided his garments among them by casting lots (ebalon kleron). Then they sat down and kept watch over him there."

The division of garments by lot directly fulfills Psalm 22:18 (LXX 21:19): "They divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." Psalm 22 is a lament of a righteous sufferer who is surrounded by enemies, pierced in hands and feet, and exposed to public shame, yet who declares his trust in God and anticipates vindication. The Psalm will be explicitly quoted by Jesus in verse 46. The author does not add a fulfillment formula here, letting the action speak for itself to the reader who recognizes the Psalm.
"And over his head they put the charge against him, which read, 'This is Jesus, the King of the Jews (houtos estin Iesous ho basileus ton Ioudaion).'"

The titulus — the placard identifying the condemned person's crime — was standard Roman practice. The charge (aitia) is kingship. The inscription is the third identification of Jesus as "King of the Jews" in the chapter (Pilate's question at v. 11, the soldiers' mockery at v. 29, and now the official Roman charge). The irony continues: the Roman legal system posts as a criminal charge what the author has been demonstrating to be true since the genealogy of chapter 1. The inscription functions simultaneously as condemnation (in Pilate's intention) and proclamation (in the author's design).
"Then two robbers were crucified with him (dyo lestai), one on the right and one on the left."

The word lestai (robbers, bandits, insurrectionists) is the term used by Josephus for the Zealot fighters and revolutionary bandits who plagued Judea (War 2.253-254). At 26:55, Jesus used the same word when he was arrested: "Have you come out as against a robber (leistes), with swords and clubs to capture me?" The placement of Jesus between two lestai presents the man who refused violent revolution (26:52, "Put your sword back into its place") being executed as one of them. Isaiah 53:12 provides the scriptural background: "He was numbered with the transgressors" (meta ton anomon elogisthe in the LXX).

"And those who passed by derided him (hoi de paraporeuomenoi eblasphemoun auton), wagging their heads (kinountes tas kephalas auton) and saying, 'You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself (soson seauton)! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.'"

The mockery from the passersby echoes Psalm 22:7 (LXX 21:8): "All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads." The verb blasphemeo (to revile, to slander) is the same word the high priest used when declaring Jesus guilty of "blasphemy" (26:65) — the charge of blasphemy is now being committed against Jesus by his mockers. The taunt "If you are the Son of God" (ei huios ei tou theou) replicates the temptation language of 4:3, 6: "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread" and "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down." The wilderness temptation and the crucifixion mockery share the same structure: a challenge to prove divine sonship by exercising power for self-preservation. In both cases, Jesus's identity as Son of God is demonstrated precisely by his refusal to act as the tempter demands.

The reference to "destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days" recalls the false testimony at 26:61. The passersby have heard a distorted version of Jesus's words and throw them back at him. The irony is that Jesus's body is the temple that will be destroyed and raised in three days (cf. John 2:19-21 for the explicit identification) — the mockers unknowingly describe what is about to happen.

"So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying, 'He saved others; he cannot save himself (allous esosen, heauton ou dynatai sosai). He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him (pisteusomen ep' auton). He trusts in God (pepoithen epi ton theon); let God deliver him now, if he desires him (ei thelei auton). For he said, "I am the Son of God."'"

The chief priests, scribes, and elders — the same groups who plotted Jesus's death (26:3-4) — now mock him publicly. Their taunt "He saved others; he cannot save himself" is another instance of unwitting truth-telling. Jesus saved others (the verb sozo — to save, to heal, to rescue — describes his healing ministry throughout the document: 9:21-22, 14:30). He "cannot save himself" not because he lacks the power but because saving himself would contradict the purpose for which he came. At 20:28, Jesus declared: "The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." Self-rescue would negate the ransom.

The taunt "let God deliver him now, if he desires him" quotes Psalm 22:8 (LXX 21:9): "He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him." The chief priests speak the words of the mocking enemies in David's psalm without recognizing that they are placing themselves in the role of the psalm's adversaries. The psalm does not end with the sufferer abandoned — it ends with vindication and universal praise (Psalm 22:22-31). By invoking the psalm's language of mockery, the religious leaders unwittingly invoke its conclusion: the sufferer will be vindicated, and "all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD" (Psalm 22:27).
"The robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way (to d' auto kai hoi lestai hoi systaurothentes syn auto oneidizon auton)."

In the author's account, even the criminals crucified alongside Jesus join the abuse. The unanimity of the mockery is total: passersby, religious leaders, and fellow condemned criminals all participate. The isolation is complete — there is no human voice raised in Jesus's defense at the cross.

div.title: The Death of Jesus and Its Attendant Signs (vv. 45-56)
div.p: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land (skotos egeneto epi pasan ten gen) until the ninth hour."

The sixth hour is noon; the ninth hour is 3:00 PM. Darkness covers "all the land" (pasan ten gen — either "all the earth" or "the whole land," with the same ambiguity as in 24:30). Three hours of midday darkness invoke the plague of darkness over Egypt in Exodus 10:22: "There was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days." They also recall Amos 8:9: "And on that day, declares the Lord GOD, I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight." In Amos, the darkness at noon accompanies God's judgment on Israel and is followed by the declaration: "I will make it like the mourning for an only son" (Amos 8:10) — the same language Zechariah 12:10 uses for the mourning over the pierced one. Joel 2:31 also connects darkened sun with the day of the LORD. The darkness is the prophetic sign of divine judgment being enacted. The cosmic disruption language Jesus used in 24:29 ("the sun will be darkened") is now physically realized at the crucifixion.

"And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice (phone megale), saying, 'Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?' that is, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (thee mou, thee mou, hina ti me egkatelipes)'"

Jesus quotes the opening verse of Psalm 22 (LXX 21:2) in Aramaic (or Hebrew, depending on the form Eli/Eloi). This is the psalm that has been providing the scriptural framework for the entire crucifixion scene: the mockery (22:7-8), the division of garments (22:18), the wagging of heads (22:7), the taunt about trusting God (22:8). By quoting its opening line, Jesus identifies himself with the psalm's speaker — the righteous sufferer who experiences abandonment by God.

The cry is not an expression of theological despair disconnected from the psalm's larger arc. In the first-century synagogue, citing the opening line of a psalm invoked the entire psalm. Psalm 22 begins with the cry of abandonment (vv. 1-2), moves through the description of suffering and mockery by enemies (vv. 6-18), and then turns decisively at verse 22: "I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you." The psalm concludes with the declaration that "all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you" (22:27), and that "posterity shall serve him; it shall be told of the Lord to the coming generation; they shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it" (22:30-31). The psalm's trajectory is from abandonment to vindication, from suffering to universal worship, from death to the proclamation of God's righteousness to future generations. Jesus's cry invokes this entire arc.
"And some of the bystanders, hearing it, said, 'This man is calling Elijah (Elian phonei houtos).'"

The mishearing of "Eli" (my God) as "Elias" (Elijah) may reflect genuine confusion between the Aramaic and the proper name, or it may be a further element of mockery. In first-century Jewish expectation, Elijah was to return before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). The suggestion that Jesus is calling for Elijah treats his cry as a plea for rescue by the eschatological forerunner.

"And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine (oxous), and put it on a reed (kalamo) and gave it to him to drink. But the rest said, 'Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him (sosonta auton).'"

The sour wine (oxos) again evokes Psalm 69:21 (LXX 68:22): "For my thirst they gave me sour wine (oxos) to drink." The offer may be an act of minimal mercy (sour wine, or posca, was a common soldier's drink) or another gesture of mockery. The reed (kalamos) — the same word used for the mock scepter in verse 29 — is now the instrument for delivering the drink. The bystanders' comment "let us see whether Elijah will come to save him" treats the moment as a spectacle, waiting to see if a miracle will intervene.
"And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit (apheken to pneuma)."

The second cry is described but its words are not recorded in this account. The verb aphiemi (to release, to send away, to let go) is used for Jesus's death: he "released his spirit" (apheken to pneuma). The language is deliberate. Jesus does not merely die; he actively releases his spirit. The verb aphiemi has been used throughout the document for forgiveness (aphiemi — to release from obligation, to forgive: 6:12, 14, 15; 9:2, 5, 6; 12:31-32; 26:28) and for leaving or departing (4:20, 22; 19:27, 29). The death is presented as a voluntary act — consistent with 20:28 ("to give his life as a ransom for many") and 26:53-54, where Jesus declared he could summon twelve legions of angels but chose not to, so that the scriptures might be fulfilled.

"And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two (to katapetasma tou naou eschisthe eis dyo), from top to bottom (ap' anothen heos kato). And the earth shook, and the rocks were split (he ge eseisthe kai hai petrai eschisthesan)."

The tearing of the temple curtain (katapetasma) is a sign of enormous significance. The naos (sanctuary, inner temple) had two curtains: one at the entrance and one separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place (the inner veil, cf. Exodus 26:31-33). The inner veil separated the place of God's presence from all human access; only the high priest entered beyond it, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2, 12-15). The tearing "from top to bottom" indicates divine agency — the direction is from God's side, not from human hands. The barrier between God's presence and the people is removed at the moment of Jesus's death. What the high priest's annual entry behind the veil symbolized — access to God and atonement for sin — is now accomplished through Jesus's death. The torn curtain declares that the temple's mediating function is superseded.

The verb schizo (to tear, to split, to rend) connects the tearing of the curtain to the earthquake that splits the rocks. The same action — splitting apart — occurs in both the sacred structure and the natural world. The earthquake (seismos — from seio, to shake) connects to the language of 24:29 where "the powers of the heavens will be shaken" (saleuthesontai). The shaking of the earth at Jesus's death is the concrete realization of the cosmic disruption the prophets associated with divine intervention.

"The tombs also were opened (ta mnemeia aneochthesan). And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised (polla somata ton kekoimemenon hagion egerthe), and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection (meta ten egersin autou) they went into the holy city and appeared to many."

This passage is unique to the author's account. The opened tombs and raised saints are presented as signs accompanying Jesus's death — though the note "after his resurrection" (meta ten egersin autou) clarifies that their appearance in Jerusalem occurred after Jesus himself was raised. The phrase "saints who had fallen asleep" (hagioi kekoimemenoi) uses the common Jewish and early Christian euphemism for death (cf. Daniel 12:2: "many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake"). The connection to Daniel 12:2 is significant: Daniel's vision of resurrection was associated with "a time of trouble, such as never has been since there was a nation" (Daniel 12:1) — the same text Jesus drew on in 24:21. The raising of the dead saints functions as a sign that Jesus's death inaugurates the eschatological reality Daniel prophesied.

The term "holy city" (hagian polin) for Jerusalem was used at 4:5, where the devil took Jesus to "the holy city" and set him on the pinnacle of the temple. The dead saints enter the holy city and are seen by many — the private event of Jesus's death produces public consequences that anticipate the general resurrection.

"When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place (ta genomena), they were filled with awe (ephoebethesan sphodra) and said, 'Truly this was the Son of God (alethos theou huios en houtos)!'"

The confession comes from the Roman centurion and his soldiers — Gentiles, agents of the occupying power, the very men who carried out the crucifixion. The phrase "Son of God" (theou huios) has been contested throughout the document: affirmed by God at the baptism (3:17) and transfiguration (17:5), confessed by Peter (16:16), used as a weapon in the temptation (4:3, 6) and in the mockers' taunts (v. 40, 43), charged as blasphemy by the Sanhedrin (26:63-65). Now it is confessed by the executioners. The word alethos (truly, really, in truth) marks this as a genuine recognition, not mockery. What the religious leaders rejected, the Gentile soldiers affirm. The pattern of the document — Gentiles recognizing what Israel's leaders do not (the magi in chapter 2, the centurion at Capernaum in 8:5-13, the Canaanite woman in 15:21-28) — reaches its climax here.

"There were also many women there (gynaikes pollai), looking on from a distance (apo makrothen theorousai), who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him (diakonousai auto). Among whom were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joseph and the mother of the sons of Zebedee."

The women are identified as those who "followed" (akoloutheo — the technical term for discipleship throughout the document: 4:20, 22; 8:22; 9:9; 19:27-28) and "ministered" (diakoneo — to serve, the same word used of the angels serving Jesus after the temptation in 4:11, and of the Son of Man who "came not to be served but to serve" in 20:28). They are present at the cross when the male disciples have fled (26:56). Their watching "from a distance" (apo makrothen) echoes Psalm 38:11 (LXX 37:12): "My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off." The women become the essential witnesses who will link the death, burial, and resurrection: they see where Jesus dies (v. 55-56), where he is buried (v. 61), and they will be the first at the empty tomb (28:1).

div.title: The Burial (vv. 57-61)
div.p: "When it was evening (opsias de genomenes), there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph (Ioseph), who also was a disciple of Jesus (hos kai autos emathetethe to Iesou). He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus (to soma tou Iesou). Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him."

Joseph is identified by three characteristics: he is rich (plousios), from Arimathea, and a disciple (matheteuo — to be a disciple, to be enrolled as a learner). The term "rich" connects to earlier teachings about wealth in the document: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God" (19:24), followed by "With God all things are possible" (19:26). Joseph of Arimathea is an example of the "possible" — a rich man who acts as a faithful disciple.

Under Roman law, the body of a crucified criminal was ordinarily left on the cross or disposed of in a common burial. Permission to claim the body required a request to the governor. Deuteronomy 21:22-23 required that the body of an executed criminal be buried before nightfall: "His body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you." Joseph's request fulfills this Torah requirement.

"And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud (sindoni kathara) and laid it in his own new tomb (en to kaino autou mnemeieo), which he had cut in the rock (ho elatomesen en te petra). And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb (prosekylisen lithon megan te thyra tou mnemeiou) and went away."

The details emphasize newness and purity: the shroud is "clean" (katharos), the tomb is "new" (kainos) — no one has been buried in it before — and it is hewn from rock (petra). The tomb carved from rock, sealed with a large stone, corresponds to the burial practices of wealthy Judeans in the first century, as attested by archaeological evidence from Jerusalem (numerous rock-cut tombs with rolling-stone closures have been excavated). The newness of the tomb ensures that no question can arise about the identity of any body found there or missing from it.

Isaiah 53:9 reads: "And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death." The Isaianic servant, condemned and killed among the wicked (cf. the two robbers, v. 38), is given burial with a rich man. Joseph of Arimathea, the rich disciple, fulfills this detail precisely.
"Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb (ekei kathemeriai apenanti tou taphou)."

The two women who witnessed the crucifixion now witness the burial. Their presence establishes the chain of testimony: they know where the body is placed. The verb kathemai (to sit) indicates they remained at the site, watching. They will return in 28:1, and their knowledge of the tomb's location ensures that the empty tomb cannot be attributed to a visit to the wrong site.

div.title: The Guard at the Tomb (vv. 62-66)
div.p: "The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation (hetis estin meta ten paraskeuen), the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate and said, 'Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive (eti zon), "After three days I will rise again (meta treis hemeras egeiromai)."'"

The temporal marker is unusual. The author does not say "on the Sabbath" but describes it indirectly as "after the day of Preparation" (paraskeue — the day before the Sabbath, when preparations for the day of rest were completed). The chief priests and Pharisees approach Pilate on the Sabbath itself, indicating the urgency they attach to the matter. The irony is once more layered: the religious leaders remember Jesus's prediction of resurrection more clearly than the disciples do. They call him "that impostor" (ho planos — the deceiver, the one who leads astray), using a word from the same root as planao (to lead astray), which Jesus applied to the false prophets in 24:4-5, 11, 24. The leaders accuse Jesus of being the deceiver, while the author has presented the leaders themselves as the ones who "lead the people astray."

"'Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day (heos tes trites hemeras), lest his disciples go and steal him away (klepsosin auton) and tell the people, "He has risen from the dead" (egerthe apo ton nekron), and the last fraud will be worse than the first (he eschate plane cheiron tes protes).'"

The chief priests anticipate the possibility that the disciples might steal the body and fabricate a resurrection story. Their concern reveals that they take Jesus's prediction seriously enough to act against it — they believe the prediction could be credibly exploited, even if they do not believe in its fulfillment. The phrase "the last fraud will be worse than the first" (he eschate plane cheiron tes protes) treats both Jesus's ministry ("the first" deception, in their view) and a potential resurrection claim ("the last" deception) as acts of plane (deception, error). This detail is narratively important because it establishes a counter-narrative that the author addresses directly at 28:11-15, where the same leaders will bribe the soldiers to say that the disciples stole the body. By reporting the guard's placement before the resurrection, the author preemptively addresses the objection: the tomb was secured, watched, and sealed, and yet it was found empty.

"Pilate said to them, 'You have a guard of soldiers (echete koustodian). Go, make it as secure as you can (asphalisasthe hos oidate).' So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard (meta tes koustodias)."

The word koustodia (guard) is a Latin loanword (custodia), indicating a Roman military guard. The sealing of the stone (sphragizo — to seal, to affix a seal) would involve a cord and wax or clay seal across the stone, so that any movement of the stone would break the seal and be immediately evident. The combination of the sealed stone and the military guard makes the tomb maximally secure by human standards. The author's point is clear: every possible precaution against tampering has been taken. The resurrection, when it occurs in chapter 28, cannot be attributed to the disciples' intervention. The security measures established by the opponents become, in the author's narrative design, evidence for the reality of what they were intended to prevent.

div.title: The Chapter's Function in the Author's Larger Argument

list.item: It completes the chain of delivery that Jesus predicted. At 20:18-19, Jesus said: "The Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day." Chapter 27 fulfills every element of this prediction in sequence: delivery to Pilate (v. 2), mockery (vv. 27-31), flogging (v. 26), and crucifixion (v. 35). The third-day rising awaits chapter 28. The narrative demonstrates that Jesus's suffering is not a defeat of his purpose but the fulfillment of it — he predicted each stage, and each stage occurs as stated.

It accumulates testimonies to Jesus's innocence from every quarter. Judas declares the blood "innocent" (v. 4). Pilate's wife calls Jesus "that righteous man" (v. 19). Pilate himself asks "What evil has he done?" and washes his hands of "this man's blood" (vv. 23-24). Even the mockers unwittingly testify to Jesus's identity: "He saved others" (v. 42), "He trusts in God" (v. 43), "He said, 'I am the Son of God'" (v. 43). The centurion confesses, "Truly this was the Son of God" (v. 54). The chapter builds its case by allowing every participant — betrayer, judge's wife, judge, enemies, and executioner — to speak truths they do not fully understand or intend.

It embeds the crucifixion in Israel's scriptural framework. The thirty pieces of silver fulfill Zechariah 11. Jesus's silence before Pilate fulfills Isaiah 53:7. The division of garments fulfills Psalm 22:18. The mockery by passersby fulfills Psalm 22:7-8. The gall and sour wine fulfill Psalm 69:21. The darkness at noon fulfills Amos 8:9. The cry of dereliction quotes Psalm 22:1. The burial with the rich man fulfills Isaiah 53:9. The author presents the death of Jesus not as an isolated event but as the convergence point of Israel's entire prophetic tradition — the righteous sufferer of the Psalms, the silent servant of Isaiah, and the rejected shepherd of Zechariah all find their referent in the same person at the same moment.

It presents Jesus's death as an act that alters the structure of Israel's worship. The tearing of the temple curtain at the moment of Jesus's death (v. 51) signals that the mediating function of the temple — its system of sacrifice, priesthood, and restricted access to God's presence — has been superseded. The curtain that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, through which only the high priest passed once a year, is torn by divine action ("from top to bottom"). The covenant blood of 26:28, poured out "for the forgiveness of sins," achieves what the temple sacrifices pointed toward. The temple whose destruction Jesus predicted in 24:2 is already rendered functionally obsolete at the moment of his death, before its physical destruction occurs forty years later.

It makes blood guilt a central narrative thread. The chapter is structured around the motif of blood: the "blood money" (time haimatos, v. 6), the "Field of Blood" (agros haimatos, v. 8), Pilate's declaration of innocence from "this man's blood" (v. 24), and the crowd's cry "His blood be on us and on our children" (v. 25). Each reference connects to the warning of 23:35-36: "Upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth... all these things will come upon this generation." The blood of Jesus, declared innocent by every witness, is the culmination of the righteous blood that has been shed throughout Israel's history. The crowd's acceptance of the blood guilt is presented by the author as the final act in the pattern of prophet-killing that Jesus denounced in chapter 23. The consequences will fall upon "this generation," as Jesus stated.

It presents the centurion's confession as a turning point in the document's ethnic scope. The Gentile soldiers' confession "Truly this was the Son of God" at the foot of the cross anticipates the universal commission of 28:19 ("make disciples of all nations"). The pattern has been building throughout the document: the Gentile magi worshipped in chapter 2, the centurion at Capernaum demonstrated faith exceeding anything in Israel (8:10), the Canaanite woman's faith was called "great" (15:28), and Jesus predicted that "many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven" (8:11). At the cross, the transition becomes explicit: Israel's leaders mock, while Gentile executioners confess. The death of Jesus breaks open the boundary of Israel's covenant to include the nations — the same dynamic that the torn curtain enacts in the cultic sphere.

It prepares for the resurrection by establishing that the death was real, witnessed, and secured against fraud. The author provides multiple layers of verification: the death is observed by the centurion and soldiers (v. 54), by the women who followed from Galilee (vv. 55-56), and by Joseph of Arimathea who handles the body (vv. 57-60). The burial location is witnessed by Mary Magdalene and the other Mary (v. 61). The tomb is sealed and guarded by Roman soldiers at the request of the chief priests (vv. 62-66). Every potential objection to the resurrection — that Jesus did not really die, that the body was moved to an unknown location, that the disciples stole it — is addressed by the narrative itself before the resurrection is reported. The chapter functions as the necessary foundation for chapter 28: the more verified the death, the more significant the empty tomb.

div.title: Matthew 28 — First-Century Reading
Context Within the Author's Argument
div.p: What came before (Matthew 27): Chapter 27 narrated the entire sequence from Jesus's delivery to Pilate through his death and burial. The chapter accumulated testimonies to Jesus's innocence from every quarter — Judas declared the blood "innocent" (27:4), Pilate's wife called Jesus "that righteous man" (27:19), Pilate himself could identify no crime (27:23) — while simultaneously embedding the crucifixion in Israel's scriptural framework: the thirty pieces of silver fulfilled Zechariah 11, Jesus's silence before Pilate fulfilled Isaiah 53:7, the division of garments and the mockery fulfilled Psalm 22, the darkness at noon fulfilled Amos 8:9, and the cry of dereliction quoted Psalm 22:1. The death was attended by signs of cosmic and covenantal significance: the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom (27:51), the earth shook, rocks split, tombs opened, and saints were raised (27:51-53). The centurion and his soldiers confessed, "Truly this was the Son of God" (27:54). The body was buried by Joseph of Arimathea in a new rock-hewn tomb, with Mary Magdalene and "the other Mary" watching where it was placed (27:61). The chapter closed with the chief priests and Pharisees securing the tomb with a Roman guard and an official seal (27:62-66), establishing every possible safeguard against tampering. The author's narrative strategy was to verify the death beyond dispute — witnessed by enemies, allies, and bystanders, sealed and guarded by the authorities who feared the very outcome the chapter is preparing to report.

What comes after: There is no chapter after Matthew 28. This is the final chapter of the document. What follows is the life of the community that the risen Jesus commissions. The document that began with "the book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham" (1:1) ends with the risen Jesus declaring universal authority and sending his disciples to "all nations" (28:19). The trajectory of the document — from Abraham's particular covenant to the inclusion of the nations — reaches its terminus. The reader is left not with an ending but with a commission: the story does not close, it opens outward.

How chapter 28 connects them: Chapter 27 established the death as real, public, and secured. Chapter 28 reports that the secured tomb is empty and the dead man is alive. The connection is not merely sequential but argumentative: the more thoroughly the death was verified and the tomb was sealed, the more significant the empty tomb becomes. The guards posted at 27:65-66 reappear at 28:4 and 28:11-15, creating a continuous narrative thread. The women who witnessed the crucifixion (27:55-56) and the burial (27:61) are the same women who arrive at the tomb (28:1), establishing an unbroken chain of testimony from death through burial to the discovery of the empty tomb. The one who was mocked as "King of the Jews" throughout chapter 27 — by the soldiers (27:29), by the inscription on the cross (27:37), by the passersby and chief priests (27:42) — now declares that "all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me" (28:18). The kingship that was parodied is real. The declaration before the Sanhedrin — "from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven" (26:64) — is vindicated: the one the Sanhedrin condemned now possesses the dominion Daniel described (Daniel 7:14). The shepherd who was struck (26:31, citing Zechariah 13:7) and whose sheep scattered (26:56) now regathers his flock in Galilee, exactly as he promised (26:32).

div.title: The Women at the Tomb and the Angel's Announcement (vv. 1-8)
div.p: "Now after the Sabbath (opse de sabbaton), toward the dawn of the first day of the week (te epiphoskouse eis mian sabbaton), Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb (elthen Mariam he Magdalene kai he alle Maria theoresai ton taphon)."

The temporal marker places the scene precisely: the Sabbath has ended, and the first day of the new week is dawning. The author has tracked time carefully through the passion: "the first day of Unleavened Bread" (26:17), "when it was evening" (26:20), "this very night" (26:34), "when morning came" (27:1), "the day of Preparation" (27:62), "the next day, after the day of Preparation" (27:62). Now it is the day after the Sabbath. Two full nights and the intervening Sabbath day have passed since the burial.

The two women — Mary Magdalene and "the other Mary" — are the same pair identified at 27:61 as sitting opposite the tomb and watching the burial. They are also among the group identified at 27:55-56 as present at the crucifixion. Their continuity across three scenes — cross, burial, tomb — establishes them as the primary witnesses whose testimony links the dead Jesus to the empty tomb. The verb theoreo (to see, to observe, to look at carefully) indicates purposeful observation, not a casual passing by. They come to "see the tomb" (theoresai ton taphon) — the text does not state that they came to anoint the body (as in Mark 16:1), only to see the place where Jesus was buried.

"And behold, there was a great earthquake (seismos megas egeneto), for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven (angelos gar kyriou katabas ex ouranou) and came and rolled back the stone (proselthon apekulisen ton lithon) and sat on it (kai ekatheto epano autou)."

The word seismos (earthquake, shaking) appeared at 27:54, where the earthquake at the moment of Jesus's death prompted the centurion's confession. The repetition of seismos connects the two events: the earth that shook when Jesus died shakes again at his vindication. The adjective megas (great) intensifies the event. In the Hebrew scriptures, earthquakes accompany theophanies — divine appearances that shake the natural order. At Sinai, "the whole mountain trembled greatly" (Exodus 19:18). In Elijah's experience at Horeb, "a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD, and after the wind an earthquake" (1 Kings 19:11). The earthquake signals that God is acting.

The angel (angelos kyriou — "angel of the Lord") descends from heaven. The phrase "angel of the Lord" (angelos kyriou) has appeared at critical moments in the document: to Joseph in a dream, announcing Jesus's conception and naming (1:20), warning him to flee to Egypt (2:13), and instructing his return (2:19-20). The angel of the Lord bracketed the beginning of Jesus's life; now the same figure appears at his emergence from death. The angel does not open the tomb to let Jesus out — the risen Jesus is not depicted as confined by the stone. The angel rolls the stone away to reveal that the tomb is already empty, and sits upon it. The rolling stone (apekulisen ton lithon), described as "great" (megan) at 27:60 when Joseph placed it, is moved by a single angelic action. The angel sits on the stone — a posture of authority and completion. What the chief priests sealed and guarded, the angel opens and occupies.
"His appearance was like lightning (he eidea autou hos astrape), and his clothing white as snow (kai to endyma autou leukon hos chion)."

The description uses language drawn from Israel's theophanic and apocalyptic tradition. Daniel 10:6 describes the angelic figure whose "face was like the appearance of lightning" (kai to prosopon autou hosei horasis astrapas in the LXX). Daniel 7:9 describes the Ancient of Days whose "clothing was white as snow" (to endyma autou hosei chion leukon). The angel at the tomb carries the visual markers of the heavenly court described in Daniel. The word astrape (lightning) appeared in Jesus's own teaching at 24:27: "For as the lightning (astrape) comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man." Lightning in the author's framework signals the breaking in of divine reality.
"And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men (apo de tou phobou autou eseisthesan hoi terountes kai egenothesan hos nekroi)."

The irony is sharp and deliberate. The guards (hoi terountes — the ones keeping watch, from tereo, to guard, to keep) who were posted to prevent any disturbance at the tomb are themselves undone by the disturbance. The verb seio (to shake, to tremble) is the same root as seismos (earthquake) — the guards are shaken as the earth is shaken. They "became like dead men" (egenothesan hos nekroi). The men stationed to guard a dead body become as dead themselves, while the dead man they were guarding is alive. The living become as dead; the dead one lives. The reversal is complete. The Roman military guard — the strongest human force available — is rendered powerless by the angelic presence. The stone, the seal, and the soldiers, which represented the full capacity of human authority to keep the tomb closed, are all overcome without resistance.

"But the angel said to the women (apokritheis de ho angelos eipen tais gynaixin), 'Do not be afraid (me phobeisthe hymeis), for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified (ton estauromenon). He is not here, for he has risen, as he said (egerththe gar kathos eipen). Come, see the place where he lay (deute idete ton topon hopou ekeito). Then go quickly and tell his disciples (tacheian poreutheisai eipate tois mathetais autou) that he has risen from the dead (hoti egerthe apo ton nekron), and behold, he is going before you to Galilee (idou proagei hymas eis ten Galilaian); there you will see him (ekei auton opsesthe). See, I have told you (idou eipon hymin).'"

The angel's address distinguishes the women from the guards: "Do not be afraid — you" (me phobeisthe hymeis). The pronoun hymeis (you, emphatic) separates them from the guards who have every reason to fear. The women came seeking Jesus; the guards were stationed to prevent anyone from finding him. The angel addresses the seekers, not the sentinels.

The identification "Jesus who was crucified" (ton estauromenon) uses the perfect passive participle — the one who was crucified and remains defined by that crucifixion. The risen one is still the crucified one. The identity is continuous: resurrection does not erase the cross but vindicates the one who hung on it.

The central declaration is "he has risen, as he said" (egerthe gar kathos eipen). The verb egeiro (to raise, to rise) is the same verb used in Jesus's predictions of his resurrection: "on the third day he will be raised" (16:21, egerthenai; 17:23, egerthesetai; 20:19, egerthesetai). The phrase "as he said" (kathos eipen) is the angel's attestation that the resurrection fulfills Jesus's own words. The document has consistently presented Jesus's predictions as coming true: the betrayal by Judas (26:21-25, fulfilled at 26:47-50), the scattering of the disciples (26:31, fulfilled at 26:56), Peter's threefold denial (26:34, fulfilled at 26:69-75), the delivery to the Gentiles (20:19, fulfilled at 27:2). The resurrection is the final prediction, and the angel's testimony is that it too has been fulfilled exactly "as he said."

The invitation "come, see the place where he lay" (deute idete ton topon hopou ekeito) turns the women into firsthand witnesses of the empty tomb. They are not told merely to believe the angel's report; they are invited to verify it with their own eyes. The tomb is open, the body is absent, and the witnesses can confirm it.

The commission to the women is threefold: go quickly (tacheian poreutheisai), tell the disciples (eipate tois mathetais), and announce the message — he has risen from the dead and is going before them to Galilee. The verb proago (to go before, to lead the way) appeared at 26:32, where Jesus told the disciples: "After I am raised up, I will go before you (proaxo hymas) to Galilee." The angel's words repeat Jesus's own promise verbatim. The scattered flock will be regathered; the shepherd who was struck is going ahead to the appointed meeting place. Galilee is where the ministry began (4:12-17), where the first disciples were called (4:18-22), and where the core of Jesus's teaching and healing took place. The risen Jesus does not summon the disciples to Jerusalem, the center of religious authority that condemned him, but to Galilee, the place of their calling.
"So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy (meta phobou kai charas megales), and ran to tell his disciples (edramon apangeilai tois mathetais autou)."

The combination of "fear and great joy" (phobou kai charas megales) is the characteristic response to theophany — the encounter with divine action produces both trembling and exhilaration. The two emotions are not contradictory but complementary: the women have witnessed something that exceeds the boundaries of ordinary experience, and the appropriate response includes both awe and elation. They run (edramon — from trecho, to run) to carry the message. The women who "followed" (akoloutheo) and "ministered" (diakoneo) during Jesus's ministry (27:55) now become the first messengers of the resurrection. The ones who remained at the cross when the male disciples fled (26:56) are the ones entrusted with the foundational announcement.

div.title: Jesus Meets the Women (vv. 9-10)
div.p: "And behold, Jesus met them (ho Iesous hypantesen autais) and said, 'Greetings! (chairete)' And they came up and took hold of his feet (ekratesan autou tous podas) and worshiped him (kai prosekynasan auto)."

The risen Jesus appears to the women while they are on their way to deliver the angel's message. The greeting chairete (rejoice, greetings) is the ordinary Greek salutation, but in this context it carries its literal force: "Rejoice!" The word chairo is the root of chara (joy), which the women already carry (v. 8). Jesus affirms and deepens their joy by his presence.

The women "took hold of his feet" (ekratesan autou tous podas). The verb krateo (to seize, to grasp, to hold) indicates physical contact — the risen Jesus has a body that can be touched and grasped. The feet are the part of the body associated with prostration and worship in the Hebrew scriptures (cf. 2 Kings 4:27, the Shunammite woman grasping Elisha's feet). The act of holding his feet combines recognition, reverence, and the tactile confirmation that this is not a vision or an apparition but a bodily presence.

The women worship him (prosekynasan auto). The verb proskyneo (to bow down, to worship, to do obeisance) has been a significant action throughout the document. The magi worshiped the child (2:11). The disciples worshiped Jesus after he walked on the sea (14:33). The Canaanite woman worshiped him (15:25). The mother of James and John worshiped him (20:20). At 4:10, Jesus declared, "You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve" (quoting Deuteronomy 6:13). The proskyneo offered to Jesus throughout the document — by magi, disciples, and supplicants — reaches its fullest expression here: the women worship the risen one without rebuke, without correction, without any indication that the worship is misdirected. The author presents the worship of the risen Jesus as the proper response.

"Then Jesus said to them, 'Do not be afraid (me phobeisthe); go and tell my brothers (hypagete apangeilate tois adelphois mou) to go to Galilee (hina apelthosin eis ten Galilaian), and there they will see me (kakei me opsontai).'"

Jesus repeats the angel's commission with one significant alteration: the angel said "tell his disciples" (tois mathetais autou, v. 7); Jesus says "tell my brothers" (tois adelphois mou). The shift from "disciples" to "brothers" is remarkable. The disciples who abandoned him (26:56), whose leader denied him three times (26:69-75), are now called "brothers" (adelphoi). The word adelphos in the document has two primary uses: biological brothers (4:18, 21; 12:46-47; 13:55) and members of the community of faith (5:22-24, 47; 7:3-5; 12:49-50; 18:15, 21, 35; 23:8; 25:40). At 12:49-50, Jesus defined his "brothers" as "whoever does the will of my Father in heaven." By calling the scattered, failed disciples "my brothers," the risen Jesus restores the relationship that their desertion had fractured. The desertion was real, but it is not the final word. The shepherd who was struck regathers the scattered sheep and names them brothers.

The destination is Galilee, repeated for the third time (26:32, 28:7, 28:10). The insistence on Galilee as the meeting place is not incidental. Galilee was the place of origins and calling; the return there after the passion constitutes a new beginning from the place of first beginnings.

div.title: The Guards' Report and the Bribery (vv. 11-15)
div.p: "While they were going (poreuomenon de auton), behold, some of the guard went into the city (tines tes koustodias elthontes eis ten polin) and told the chief priests all that had taken place (apangeilan tois archiereusin hapanta ta genomena)."

The narrative now follows two tracks simultaneously: the women are going to the disciples with the message of resurrection, and the guards are going to the chief priests with the same report. Both groups witnessed the same events — the earthquake, the angel, the open tomb. Both report what happened. The word apangeilan (reported, announced) is the same verb used for the women's mission to the disciples (apangeilai, v. 8). The parallel is deliberate: the testimony goes to both the believing community and to the hostile authorities. The facts are the same; the response will differ.

"And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel (symboulion labontes), they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers (argyria hikana edokan tois stratiotais), saying, 'Tell people, "His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were sleeping" (hoi mathetai autou nyktos elthontes eklepsan auton hemon koimomenon).'"

The phrase "assembled with the elders and taken counsel" (symboulion labontes) echoes 27:1, where the same groups "took counsel" (symboulion elabon) to put Jesus to death. The same phrase marks the same pattern: the religious leadership responds to a crisis by conspiring. Having failed to keep Jesus in the tomb, they now attempt to control the narrative about why it is empty.

The word argyria (silver, money) recalls the "thirty pieces of silver" (triakonta argyria) paid to Judas at 26:15. Silver was the currency of betrayal in this narrative; now silver is the currency of suppression. Judas was paid silver to deliver Jesus to death; the guards are paid silver to deny that he has risen from it. The adjective hikana (sufficient, considerable) indicates that the bribe was large enough to ensure compliance.

The fabricated story — "his disciples came by night and stole him away while we were sleeping" — is internally contradictory, a point the author expects the reader to notice. If the guards were sleeping, they could not know what happened to the body. If they were awake, they could not claim the disciples overpowered a Roman military guard. The story is designed not for logical coherence but for public circulation. The author has already established at 27:62-66 that the chief priests themselves requested the guard precisely because they feared the disciples might steal the body. Having established the guard against that possibility, the chief priests now invent the very scenario they sought to prevent, as the cover story for what actually occurred.
"'And if this comes to the governor's ears (ean akousthe touto epi tou hegemonos), we will satisfy him (hemeis peisomen auton) and keep you out of trouble (hymas amerimnous poiesomen).'"

Sleeping on guard duty was a capital offense in the Roman military (Polybius, Histories 6.37). The chief priests promise to protect the soldiers from the consequences of the story they are being told to tell. The verb peitho (to persuade, to satisfy) was used at 27:20 for the chief priests "persuading" (epeisan) the crowd to ask for Barabbas. The same verb marks the same tactic: the chief priests use persuasion — here combined with money — to control the outcome. The word amerimnous (free from care, without anxiety) appeared at 6:25, 31, 34, in Jesus's teaching about anxiety: "Do not be anxious" (me merimnate). The chief priests promise freedom from anxiety — but the freedom they offer is the freedom of complicity in a lie, not the freedom from fear that the angel and the risen Jesus offered to the women (28:5, 10).

"So they took the money and did as they were directed (edidachthesan). And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day (diephemsthe ho logos houtos para Ioudaiois mechri tes semeron hemeras)."

The verb didasko (to teach, to instruct) appears in the passive: the soldiers "were instructed" (edidachthesan). The irony is that the word for what the chief priests do to the soldiers is the same word used for what Jesus does with his disciples — both "teach." But the content is opposite: Jesus teaches truth; the chief priests teach a fabrication.

The editorial note "to this day" (mechri tes semeron hemeras) is the author's address to the first-century reader. This phrase appeared at 27:8 regarding the "Field of Blood" and signals a present-tense reality known to the author's audience. The author acknowledges that the counter-narrative — the claim that the disciples stole the body — is actively circulating at the time of writing. The entire passage (27:62-66 through 28:11-15) functions as the author's response to this specific objection: the tomb was guarded and sealed; the guards witnessed the events; the guards were bribed to lie; the lie is still being told. The author does not merely assert the resurrection; he addresses the most prominent alternative explanation and argues that it was fabricated by the same authorities who engineered the crucifixion.

The phrase "among the Jews" (para Ioudaiois) reflects the perspective of a community that distinguishes itself from the broader Jewish population that has not accepted the resurrection claim. The phrase does not denote an ethnic category from outside but an intra-communal distinction: those who follow Jesus and those who follow the teaching of the chief priests have parted ways on this foundational question.

div.title: The Risen Jesus on the Mountain in Galilee (vv. 16-20)
div.p: "Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee (hoi de hendeka mathetai eporeuthsan eis ten Galilaian), to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them (eis to oros hou etaxato autois ho Iesous)."

The number "eleven" (hendeka) rather than "twelve" (dodeka) silently registers Judas's absence. The twelve were constituted at 10:1-4; now they are eleven. The gap in the number is the permanent scar of the betrayal. The text does not explain what happened to Judas — the reader already knows from 27:5 that he hanged himself. The eleven are what remains of the community that Jesus called and formed.

They go to Galilee, as instructed three times (26:32, 28:7, 28:10), and to a specific mountain (to oros — the mountain) "to which Jesus had directed them" (hou etaxato autois). The verb tasso (to appoint, to direct, to assign) indicates a prior arrangement — Jesus specified this location. The document does not identify which mountain, but mountains have served as sites of revelation and commission throughout the text. The Sermon on the Mount was delivered from a mountain (5:1). Jesus went up on a mountain to pray (14:23). The transfiguration occurred on "a high mountain" (17:1). The eschatological discourse was given on the Mount of Olives (24:3). In the Hebrew scriptures, mountains are the places where God meets his people and delivers his commands: Sinai (Exodus 19-20), Horeb (1 Kings 19), Zion (Psalm 2:6, Isaiah 2:2-3). The mountain in Galilee continues this pattern: the risen Jesus meets his reconstituted community on a mountain and delivers his final commission, as Moses received the Torah on Sinai and delivered it to Israel.
"And when they saw him they worshiped him (kai idontes auton proseknyesan), but some doubted (hoi de edistasan)."

The response is divided: worship and doubt exist simultaneously. The verb proskyneo (to worship) continues the pattern from verse 9, where the women worshiped the risen Jesus. Now the eleven also worship. But the author adds the striking note: hoi de edistasan — "but some doubted." The verb distazo (to doubt, to hesitate, to waver) appeared only once before in the document, at 14:31, when Peter began to sink while walking on the water and Jesus said, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?" (eis ti edistasas). The word describes not outright disbelief but divided conviction — the wavering between trust and uncertainty, the inability to commit fully to what the senses report and the mind struggles to accept.

The author's inclusion of the doubt is remarkable. This is the final scene of the document, the culminating moment, and the author does not present it as a scene of unanimous, triumphant faith. Some worship; some waver. The honesty of the detail argues against fabrication — a writer inventing this scene for propaganda purposes would not include doubt among the witnesses at the climactic moment. The detail also connects to the document's consistent portrayal of the disciples as people of "little faith" (oligopistoi, 6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8; 17:20). Even the resurrection does not instantly resolve the disciples' struggle to trust. The community that will receive the commission is not a community of perfect faith but a community of worshipers who still wrestle with uncertainty.
"And Jesus came and said to them (kai proselthon ho Iesous elalesen autois legon), 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (edothe moi pasa exousia en ourano kai epi ges).'"

Jesus approaches them (proselthon — he comes to them, not they to him) and speaks. The first word of the commission is a declaration of authority. The verb didomi (to give) is in the aorist passive: "has been given" (edothe). The passive voice indicates that the authority comes from God — it is the Father who gives, as at 11:27: "All things have been delivered to me by my Father (panta moi paredothe hypo tou patros mou)." The scope is total: "all authority" (pasa exousia), in "heaven and on earth" (en ourano kai epi ges). No domain is excluded. The word exousia (authority, power, right to act) has been contested and demonstrated throughout the document: authority to forgive sins (9:6), authority over unclean spirits (10:1), the question of by what authority Jesus acts (21:23-27), and the authority of the Son of Man enthroned at God's right hand (26:64).

This declaration directly fulfills Daniel 7:13-14. In Daniel's vision, "one like a son of man" comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion: "And to him was given (edothe auto in the LXX) dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed." The verbal and conceptual parallels are exact: authority is "given" (edothe) to the Son of Man, it extends over all domains, and it encompasses "all peoples, nations, and languages." At 26:64, Jesus declared to the Sanhedrin that they would see "the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven." The Sanhedrin's response was to condemn him to death. Now, on the mountain in Galilee, the condemned one announces that the Daniel 7 investiture has taken place. The authority the Sanhedrin rejected has been conferred by the one whose authority the Sanhedrin cannot touch.

"'Go therefore and make disciples of all nations (poreuthentes oun matheteusate panta ta ethne), baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (baptizontes autous eis to onoma tou patros kai tou huiou kai tou hagiou pneumatos), teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you (didaskontes autous terein panta hosa eneteilamen hymin).'"

The word oun (therefore) is crucial: because all authority has been given to Jesus, therefore the disciples are sent. The commission flows from the authority. The imperative is matheteusate (make disciples) — from matheteuo, the same verb used to describe Joseph of Arimathea as one who "had been made a disciple" (ematheuthe, 27:57). The verb appeared at 13:52 for the "scribe trained (matheutheisas) for the kingdom of heaven." To "make disciples" is to do what Jesus did when he called the fishermen at 4:18-22, when he called Matthew at 9:9, and when he formed the twelve at 10:1-4 — to draw people into the relationship of learning, following, and obedience that defines a mathetetes (learner, disciple).

The scope is "all nations" (panta ta ethne). The phrase panta ta ethne has appeared at decisive moments in the document: at 24:9 ("you will be hated by all nations"), at 24:14 ("this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations"), and at 25:32 ("before him will be gathered all the nations"). The trajectory has been building since the opening genealogy, which included Gentile women (Rahab, Ruth) in Jesus's lineage (1:5), through the magi from the east (2:1-12), through the centurion whose faith surpassed all in Israel (8:10), through Jesus's declaration that "many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven" (8:11), through the Canaanite woman's great faith (15:28), and through the centurion's confession at the cross (27:54). The boundary of Israel's covenant is now explicitly opened to include every nation. The particularism of 10:5-6 ("Go nowhere among the Gentiles... but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel") and 15:24 ("I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel") was the appointed scope for the earthly ministry; the commission of the risen Jesus extends the mission to every people.

The formula "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" brings together three identifications that have appeared throughout the document. The Father has been identified as the source of Jesus's authority (11:27), the one whose will Jesus submits to (6:10, 26:39, 42), and the one who has revealed Jesus's identity (3:17, 16:17, 17:5). The Son has been identified as the one through whom the Father is known (11:27), confessed by Peter (16:16) and the centurion (27:54), and declared by God himself (3:17, 17:5). The Holy Spirit has been present at Jesus's conception (1:18, 20), his baptism (3:16), his temptation (4:1), and his teaching about blasphemy against the Spirit (12:31-32). The formula does not explain the relationship among the three; it names the reality into which the baptized person is brought. The word onoma (name) in Jewish usage represents the person's identity and character — to be baptized "into the name" (eis to onoma) is to be brought into the reality the name represents.

The instruction "teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you" (didaskontes autous terein panta hosa eneteilamen hymin) points back to the content of Jesus's teaching throughout the document. The verb entellomai (to command, to charge) is the word used for authoritative instruction. The word panta (all) — "all that I have commanded" — encompasses the entire body of Jesus's teaching: the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5-7), the mission discourse (chapter 10), the parables of the kingdom (chapter 13), the community discourse (chapter 18), and the eschatological discourse (chapters 23-25). The five great teaching blocks of the document are the content of what the disciples are to teach the nations. The verb tereo (to keep, to observe, to guard) indicates not merely hearing but doing — the practical obedience that has been the standard of genuine discipleship since 7:24-27, where the wise person is the one who "hears these words of mine and does them." The commission is not merely to spread information but to form communities of obedience.
"'And behold, I am with you always (kai idou ego meth' hymon eimi), to the end of the age (heos tes synteleias tou aionos).'"

The final words of the document form an inclusio — a literary bracket — with the first chapter. At 1:23, the author cited Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel (Emmanouel), which means, God with us (meth' hemon ho theos)." The document that began with the declaration that the child would be called "God with us" ends with the risen Jesus declaring "I am with you" (ego meth' hymon eimi). The promise of divine presence that Isaiah announced and Matthew applied to Jesus at his birth is now spoken by Jesus himself at his commissioning of the community. The document's christological claim is stated in its opening and closing frames: Jesus is the presence of God with his people.

The phrase "I am" (ego eimi) carries resonance from the Hebrew scriptures. At Exodus 3:14, God identified himself to Moses as "I AM" (ego eimi ho on in the LXX).
